articles.title_zh: S&P 500 is little changed as tech stock losses outweigh cooler oil prices ahead of midterms: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell sharply Monday as the presidents of the U.S. and Iran signal they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, fell 7.7% to $104.66 a barrel as of 12:11 p.m. ET. U.S. West Texas Intermediate declined 7.3% to $96.50 per barrel.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections.
The president "hasn't made a decision," Rubio told reporters over the weekend.
"What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it," the secretary of State said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is seeking to resolve problems through dialogue, according to state-owned Islamic Republic News Agency . Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has granted the government certain authorities to do this, Pezeshkian said.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said an agreement with the U.S. is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill" and is "truly seeking a peaceful solution," according to IRNA.
Araghchi said mediators are discussing the proposal Iran made during the United Nations General Assembly in September. Tehran expects the U.S. to lift sanctions, reduce its military presence in the region to previous levels and lift the blockade, the foreign minister said.
But Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Reports about diplomatic efforts will have a big impact on crude oil prices because much of the market's recent gains were risk premium in anticipation of a possible escalation, according to Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.
"With that said, so long as there is no concrete conclusion to the war, and tanker and Houthi attacks remain prevalent, we do not anticipate a complete erosion of the risk premium via diplomacy headlines alone," McKay said.
— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Iran says "ball is in the U.S. court" on deal to end war as Trump keeps his intentions veiled
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran says "ball is in the U.S. court" on deal to end war as Trump keeps his intentions veiled
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing for another wave of strikes on Iran after Tuesday's midterm elections in the U.S., according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter, each of whom spoke with the Associated Press. Their comments followed an earlier report from Axios, which cited sources who said Netanyahu had pushed for President Trump to strike Iran during a call between the two leaders over the weekend, but Mr. Trump wanted to let the negotiations play out.
The two regional officials told AP that diplomatic efforts have made progress, with Qatari mediators holding two rounds of talks last week with Iranian officials. Both officials said the mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade on Iran's ports.
They said more talks are planned for this week. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American, and in one case Israeli, officials.
One official said Netanyahu was working with senior officials in the U.S. administration to persuade Trump to launch a quick but extensive air campaign and that the president does not appear to have made a decision.
Other U.S. allies in the Middle East are warning against more strikes, saying it would destabilize the region and could lead Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen to step up their attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping, a third regional official said. Iran-backed militias in Iraq could also get involved.
That official wasn't authorized to speak publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.
The Israeli government did not immediately comment. The White House did not directly respond to questions about Netanyahu and Trump's discussion of potential new strikes during the weekend call.
Iran's vice president said on Monday that exchanges with the U.S. via mediators indicated Washington's recognition of Tehran's "victory" in the Middle East war, Iranian state media reported.
"Our enemy failed to achieve any of its objectives in the last two wars. Even today, although the United States, driven by its own goals and concerns regarding domestic public opinion, is engaging in various maneuvers, the messages conveyed to Iran through intermediaries point to an acknowledgment of our victory," said Iran's First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref, according to IRNA state news agency.
Oil prices sank around seven percent on Monday, the eve of crucial midterm elections in the U.S., as signals that Tehran and Washington were renewing dialogue boosted hopes of ending the Middle East war.
Earlier, Axios outlet reported that Vice President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks, in the highest-level move from the Trump administration in months.
Arne Lohmann Rasmussen, chief analyst at Global Risk Management, told AFP that her organization believes such signals from the administration "may be tactical" ahead of the midterms.
"Meanwhile, attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz continue [and] we maintain our higher-for-longer outlook for energy prices," Rasmussen said.
But share prices of energy majors have dropped, while many other sectors were boosted by the cooling fuel costs. Stocks got a lift from sharp drops in oil prices, which headed back down in their latest yo-yo move on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global industry to return to normal. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, fell 7.4% to $105.03.
The price for the most actively traded contract in the Brent market has been veering between roughly $70 and $120 per barrel since just before the war began, and it's been quick to reverse direction.
Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, a military spokesperson for the Iran-backed Houthis, said Monday that the Saudi coalition fighting the rebel group in Yemen had launched more than 100 airstrikes over the course of the last day.
"Saudi warplanes launched 109 airstrikes over the past 24 hours," the spokesperson said in a statement shared on X. The strikes targeted the Yemeni provinces of Saada, Taiz, Lahj, Al-Jawf, and Hodeidah, according to the statement. Some of those provinces are in Houthi-controlled or contested territories.
The spokesperson said airstrikes between Sunday and Monday brought the total number of Saudi strikes and missile attacks to 3,939 since the fighting in Yemen escalated earlier this fall.
Saree's latest comments came after he claimed in another statement Monday that the Houthis had carried out new attacks against Saudi Arabian infrastructure, including a civilian airport, over the last 48 hours.
A spokesman for the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed Monday that the group had carried out new attacks over the preceding 48 hours on Saudi Arabian infrastructure, including a civilian airport.
Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesman, said in a statement shared on social media that the group had struck Saudi Arabia's eastern Dammam Airport  "using two drones, and the operation achieved its objective successfully, resulting in the disruption of air traffic at the airport."
He said another drone hit an "early warning radar in Jizan," a city on Saudi Arabia's western Red Sea coast, while unspecified Houthi weapons hit "a military transport aircraft at Jizan Airport."
The Houthis have peppered Saudi Arabia's airports and energy infrastructure for weeks in retaliation for the kingdom's backing of Yemen's government in the impoverished Middle Eastern nation's grueling decade-long civil war. Iran has long backed the Houthis as a powerful proxy force, particularly as a counter to Iran's arch-foe Saudi Arabia, which shares a long border with Yemen.
Houthi drone and missile strikes last month killed at least 20 people at Saudi airports , and despite the kingdom's vast military and financial advantage over the rebels, it has been unable to stop the attacks .
There was no immediate information from Saudi officials to confirm or deny Saree's claims on Monday.
The Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, had a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Monday, Iranian state media reported, in a continuation of recent talks between the two countries about the situation in the Middle East.
During their call, Rezaei and Putin discussed regional and global affairs, focusing on West Asia and ongoing "strategic cooperation" between Iran and Russia, according to Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency.
Iran and Russia have long been allies, and their relationship has been cemented during both the ongoing Russian assault on Ukraine, and the U.S. war with Iran. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in October that Tehran's ties with Russia were closer than ever, contradicting Mr. Trump's assertion at the time that Moscow was "doing very little, if anything, to help" Tehran amid the war.
According to Tasnim, Rezaei thanked Putin Monday for Russia's support.
Iran's top diplomat said Monday that negotiations with the U.S., via mediators, aimed at reaching an agreement to end the war have been "proceeding very intensively," but he added that "everything depends on Washington's political rationality," according to Iran's state news agency IRNA.
IRNA quoted Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi as reiterating that Tehran will not back down from its conditions for a deal to end the war and to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Closed-door negotiations have taken place via mediators, primarily Qatar and Pakistan, and Iranian officials said earlier Monday that it would be up to the U.S. side to make a move and end the monthslong standoff sparked by the joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Feb. 28.

articles.title_orig: Apple earnings live updates: New CEO John Ternus faces first Wall Street test
articles.title_zh: Apple earnings live updates: New CEO John Ternus faces first Wall Street test
articles.content_orig:
It's not just the neoclouds and hyperscalers that investors are anxious about.
Options data show a surge in bearish trading in anticipation of both Palantir and Apple earnings Monday afternoon. The two stocks have been on trajectories that are distinct from the broader AI trade – with Apple, in particular, trading almost inversely to the Nasdaq 100 Index – but that's not stopping speculators from betting on a reversal in their shares after earnings.
Of the 620,000 options traded on Apple by midday, 385,000 were puts, with at least 113,000 puts likely initiated by buyers, compared to just 64,000 calls bought, Cboe LiveVol data show. At the same time, the price of puts reached the 86th percentile of the past year, compared to the 51st percentile for calls, according to data from Nations Indexes.
Apple stock is up 25% this year and currently trading with a negative 0.65 correlation with the Nasdaq 100, ThinkOrSwim data show. Options are implying just under a 4% move for the stock, compared to the average 2.5% swing after earnings the past two years, according to LiveVol.
Palantir options flows are also leaning bearish, with more puts trading than calls by volume and the price of puts at the 97th percentile of the past year, according to Nations Indexes. Calls are pricey, too, but not as much – they're in the 76th percentile.
Traders should be ready for a big move in Palantir: market-makers are pricing an 11.5% implied move, compared to the 10% average the past two years. The stock rallied almost 30% after its last report, but sold off after earnings in May.
The biggest trade in Palantir Monday was someone opening a new position buying about 750 in-the-money 250-strike puts expiring mid-February for a total $5.1 million.

articles.title_orig: Marvell doubles down on AI boom with costly $115 billion Lumentum deal
articles.title_zh: Marvell doubles down on AI boom with costly $115 billion Lumentum deal
articles.content_orig:
Marvell Technology 's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday.
"You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here."
Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release.
Marvell shares slumped 8% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank 13%.
Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models.
"We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Murphy said.
Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028.
Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending.
This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology.
Marvell 's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies.
In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers.
"This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them."
Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone.
CORRECTION: This story has been updated to reflect that Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston described the deal as an 'enormous' opportunity. A previous version of this story incorrectly cited the Marvell CEO.

articles.title_orig: Mercedes Sales Plunge 31% in China as It Eyes Bigger US Push
articles.title_zh: Mercedes Sales Plunge 31% in China as It Eyes Bigger US Push
articles.content_orig:
China sales fell 31% last quarter, yet Mercedes says it is “indispensable” and plans to build future Chinese-market cars almost entirely with local parts.
2027 Mercedes-Benz CLA 220 Hybrid in Manufaktur Patagonia Red
Mercedes-Benz , though currently struggling to retain market position in China, says it will give a broader 2030 strategy update, which will include a detailed review of its China business, next year. The numbers explain the urgency: German brands have been getting crushed in China .
Mercedes-Benz is doubling down on the market that is hurting it most. According to Reuters , CEO Ola Källenius calls China an “indispensable market and innovation hub.
Third-quarter Mercedes-Benz Cars sales fell 8 percent to 407,232, with China down 31 percent to 86,800, according to BigGo . Elsewhere, Europe was up 5 percent, Germany was up 13 percent, and the US was up 6 percent, with record battery-electric sales up 61 percent. Adjusted return on sales for cars dropped to 2.5 percent from 4.8 percent, and Mercedes cut its full-year guidance to 2-3 percent from 3-5 percent; its CFO called the fourth quarter “a break-even quarter.”
Starting with the electric E-Class in the second half of 2027, Källenius said Mercedes will source “almost everything” in China for Chinese production. According to reports, CFO Harald Wilhelm also wants the company to rely less on China as a profit source. That is a split-screen strategy: stay in the world’s largest car market, but with local suppliers and less exposure to its price war. Mercedes has already felt that pain from tariffs and China’s EV boom.
If you live in the US, this is the good-news part. The China sourcing applies to cars built for China, and nothing in the reporting says it changes what’s sold here. What matters more is where Mercedes is growing: US sales rose 6 percent last quarter, and Källenius said the company plans further US investments and sees potential to lift annual sales from more than 300,000 vehicles toward 400,000, per Reuters. Audi announced a $4 billion US assembly plant that will create around 4,500 jobs. Mercedes too is changing gears in a push for higher volume after years of sliding sales. For buyers, that could mean more attention and more incentives, though nothing has been promised.
In Germany, Mercedes will relaunch a voluntary severance program for indirect staff from December. It booked about €1.8 billion (about $2 billion) in provisions for the last round in 2025, with most of the new program’s earnings impact expected in 2027. Källenius said further German investment depends on productivity and costs, noting US labor costs run at roughly 80 percent of German levels.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Shares of Micron (NASDAQ:MU) stumbled out of the gate Friday morning, falling as much as 5.9%. As of 11:28 a.m. ET, the stock was still down 4.7%.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
The catalyst that sent the semiconductor specialist lower was a competitor's bullish financial report, which wasn't enough to ease investor concerns about the future of artificial intelligence (AI).
Image source: The Motley Fool.
Rival memory chipmaker Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) released its financial results, which were by all accounts bullish. For its fiscal 2027 first quarter (ended Oct. 2), the company delivered revenue that soared 378% year over year and 23% quarter over quarter to $11 billion. This fueled adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $49.51, which grew more than 40-fold.
For context, analysts' consensus estimates were for revenue of $10.7 billion and adjusted EPS of $46.67, so the company cleared both hurdles by a wide margin.
Unrelenting demand for the memory chips that underpin AI continued. Data center revenue was the highlight, surging 1,682% year over year to $4.8 billion, while edge computing revenue of $5.8 billion jumped 320%.
Sandisk even provided a robust second-quarter forecast that surpassed Wall Street's expectations, guiding for revenue of $12.4 billion and adjusted gross margin of 85%, both at the midpoint of its guidance.
On the heels of its stellar financial report, Sandisk stock plunged as much as 11% on Friday, dragging other memory chipmakers down with it.
The reason for the stalling stock prices is complex. Sandisk and Micron stocks have gained 488% and 293%, respectively, over the past year, driven higher by surging demand for the memory chips used for AI. After runs of this magnitude, investors are increasingly concerned that the good times can't last -- particularly when it comes to AI.
Moreover, the Big Three memory chipmakers -- Sandisk, Micron, and SK Hynix -- tend to move together, and that phenomenon held true today.
Finally, Micron stock is selling for just 12 times earnings. For investors who believe that AI still has room to run, this represents an attractive buying opportunity.

articles.title_zh: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).
It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.
In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.
Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.
In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce.
The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".
In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit.
A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.
In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.
The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.
The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.
In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.
A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.
A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.
Additional reporting by Shiona McCallum

articles.title_orig: U.S. economy could lose $1B as gamers plan to rob liquor stores, steal cars
articles.title_zh: U.S. economy could lose $1B as gamers plan to rob liquor stores, steal cars
articles.content_orig:
The "Grand Theft Auto" videogame franchise is notorious for its in-game heists — and now managers can add "stealing productivity" to its list of crimes when the long-awaited "Grand Theft Auto VI" drops on Thursday, Nov. 19, after years of delays.
Amy Gettler, who has taken the day off from work for every "GTA" release, is one of the millions of fans who's been waiting for "GTA 6" since playing the previous version in 2013. Gettler, 43, has already preordered the game, which rings in at $79.99 (or $99.99 for the "ultimate edition" with extra digital content, like custom cars), and asked for paid time off on the Thursday release date. She and her husband, who's also taking the 19th off, plan to spend five to eight hours playing that day.
My wife cried when I found out she had only $80,000 in her 401(k). I have $2.2 million. Am I wrong to be shocked?
Your stock portfolio increasingly hinges on the bond market — and the midterm elections
The stock market's front-runners stumbled in October. Here's where the smart money is moving now.
80% of workers make this 401(k) mistake when they retire
"We are going to park ourselves in front of our TV in the living room — we got a new TV, a 65-inch," she said. "I'm going to dedicate as much time as I can to it. I'm going to let hours float by."
They're not alone. Almost one-fifth (18%) of American workers plan to take Nov. 19 off to play "GTA 6," according to Bamboo HR, drawing on its platform data from more than 3.4 million U.S.-based employees and surveys from over 1,500 workers. The human-resource platform also finds that the paid-time-off request rate for the game's release date is 13% higher than it was on similar days last year and in 2024.
What's more, a widely-shared International Business Times report has even claimed that "GTA 6" could cost the U.S. economy $1 billion in lost productivity in a single day — although it should be noted that this estimate seems to have been worked out by a Barcelona economics professor, and was not taken from a published paper.
And 32% of respondents to MarketWatch's own polls on Instagram and X said they plan to take the day off — or, secretly play the game while on the clock, perhaps while they're working from home.
In fact, the CEO of Take-Two Interactive Software TTWO — the parent company of "GTA 6" developer Rockstar Games — even told gaming news site IGN earlier this year that he thinks "a lot of people will be calling in sick on Nov. 19."
Buzz around the game has also spawned viral "Saturday Night Live" sketches, and YouTube skits about droves of workers all putting in for the same time off in order to play the game.
"South Park" even revealed an exclusive sneak peek of "GTA 6" footage during its most recent episode on Thursday.
"Being such a fan, and waiting 13 years for this game to come out and the hype around it, I don't want to wait to play it until the weekend," Gettler said. And besides: "After work, I'm drained."
So what's making "GTA 6" the most hotly anticipated game of the year — if not the past decade?
Nearly one in three American console and PC gamers plan to buy "GTA 6," according to new Circana data — the highest level of purchase intent for a videogame in the global market-research firm's tracking history.
"Players have been waiting 13 years for a sequel to 'Grand Theft Auto V,' and demand is expected to extend beyond software sales to include consoles, accessories and gaming subscriptions as consumers prepare for launch," Circana's videogames industry analyst Mat Piscatella said in a statement.
"The game is unique and such a cultural phenomenon," said Karl Kontus , a senior vice president of videogame insights at Sensor Tower. "It's not just a game. It's something you talk to your friends about and brag about."
Additions like a full bus system, detailed non-player characters and a much, much larger map all have gamers itching to start playing. This is also the longest amount of time gamers have had to wait for a new "GTA" game. The previous record was five years between the release of "GTA 4" and "GTA 5," so there's 13 years of pent-up demand at play.
And that hype is translating into huge presales. Six weeks before the release date, there were already almost 7 million pre-orders for "GTA 6," according to data from Sensor Tower as of Friday, raking in over $600 million already. That is 148% higher than the number of presale orders that "Call of Duty: Modern Warfare II," the next-best-selling game of the past six years, had this far out from its release date.
The long-term trajectory of sales for a game like this once it finally hits store shelves is "incredibly big," said Kontus.
"It's in a league of its own, so it's hard to benchmark it against anything else," he added. "Some of the biggest preorders that have been publicly announced … achieved 8 million preorders by launch. 'GTA 6' is going to completely blow past that number. It's going to, at the very least, double what it is right now."
It's likely to be twice as popular as its predecessor, "GTA 5," which came out in 2013 and had 7 million presales, according to data from VGChartz . Sales passed the $1 billion mark just three days after that game's release.
Previously: 'GTA 6' preorders are live — and pack an unpleasant surprise for gamers besides the $80 price tag
"GTA 6" is also hitting shelves at the perfect time to take time off from work — a week before Thanksgiving, and during a month when people are more willing and maybe more eager to use their remaining time off before the end of the year. Last year, 62% of Americans didn't use all their paid time off, according to data from Vacation Tracker.
What's more, the rise in remote work has made it so many workers don't necessarily have to take a full day off to play the new game — such as remote workers planning take a "soft off" day.
Take Jeffery Haynes, 40, who said he is allotting four to five hours to playing "GTA 6" on Nov. 19 — including during work hours. He's been a fan of the game since he was in high school.
"I plan to play after work, but I'll play while I'm 'working,' too, since I work from home," he said.
For the uninitiated, "GTA 6" will be a huge, open-world game giving its players plenty to do in the days and weeks — if not months — to come. So the distraction from work could run beyond just a single day.
"I'm excited to 'lock in' on a videogame," Haynes added, "which I haven't done since 'GTA 5' came out."

articles.title_orig: King's role is not policy making, says Palace in slavery apology row
articles.title_zh: King's role is not policy making, says Palace in slavery apology row
articles.content_orig:
The King's role as head of the Commonwealth is about "inspiring and convening, rather than policy making", says Buckingham Palace - distancing him from rows over whether the UK should apologise and make reparations for its part in the Atlantic slave trade.
The Palace statement clarifying the King's non-political role in the Commonwealth comes as the organisation's leaders gather for a summit in Antigua and Barbuda.
The King is to deliver a speech on Tuesday which is expected to recognise the painful legacy of slavery. But his speech will reflect the position of the UK government.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had suggested there could be some form of apology over slavery, but has ruled out financial reparations.
The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.
On Saturday, the prime minister said that the UK "must face up to the past" over the "brutal and barbaric violation" of the slave trade, and that he was "open" to the possibility of a formal apology.
But on Monday, his official spokesperson said that while Burnham had "expressed his sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering caused by the transatlantic slave trade", this was "distinct from a formal apology".
Burnham thought it was "right that a formal apology is discussed properly with the countries and communities most affected", his spokesperson said.
"An apology of this significance should be informed by the people and countries most affected," they added.
Meanwhile Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK was "self-confident enough to have this conversation".
"The dialogue we're setting up will consider whether and how a formal apology could help acknowledge the history, help heal the division and support stronger relationships for the future," he said.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has rejected "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from solving the UK's current problems.
Gaston Brown, Prime Minister of Antigua and Barbuda, the country which is hosting the Commonwealth gathering, says that the consequences of slavery "have not disappeared with the passage of time" and wants to discuss reparations.
Whichever way the King's speech addresses the subject of slavery will be a political decision.
On previous occasions, the King has used strong language, such as talking about his "greatest sorrow and regret" at the "abhorrent and unjustifiable acts of violence" of the colonial era on a visit to Kenya.
And in Antigua he is expected to voice his "sincere sorrow", having spoken about the "great suffering of the past" in the Bahamas last week.
But any formal apology and any action on reparations on behalf of the UK would be a decision for political leaders - and the statement from the Palace defuses any expectation of such an intervention.
Instead the Palace sets out the King's role as a unifying figure above such divisions, with the Commonwealth described as a "family" of nations.
The King's "most significant contribution has been helping to connect leaders, institutions and investors - many of whom he knows personally from his many years of international diplomacy", says the Palace.
And that relates to "shared areas of interest and concern, creating the conditions in which ambitious Commonwealth-led initiatives can emerge and succeed".
It's a view of a positive and collective approach of the King's role in the Commonwealth, bringing together politicians with business leaders, philanthropists and civil society.

articles.title_orig: China releases timeline for lunar landing on the Moon, targeting "before 2030"
articles.title_zh: China releases timeline for lunar landing on the Moon, targeting "before 2030"
articles.content_orig:
Chinese space officials confirmed this weekend that the Asian nation plans to land its astronauts on the Moon within three years.
At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, officials, including Wang Xiang, chief designer for the lunar exploration program, laid out the country’s most publicly detailed plans yet for a series of missions leading up to a crewed lunar landing “before 2030.”
China’s lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon.
According to slides shared on social media, the current plan involves:
The public release of this new information provides a timeline for gauging China’s technical progress in its efforts to land humans on the Moon before 2030 and beat NASA and the United States back to the lunar surface.
Notably, the plan (for now, at least) omits a mission similar to Apollo 8 or Artemis II, which involved a crew flying out to the Moon and either entering orbit or passing close by before returning to Earth. The Mengzhou vehicle should still get a workout closer to Earth with humans on board as part of missions carrying astronauts to Tiangong, China’s space station in low-Earth orbit.
NASA has set a target of landing humans on the Moon by 2028, a year or so ahead of China. The United States, which has been working on the Space Launch System rocket for 15 years and the Orion spacecraft even longer, has a more established rocket and crew vehicle.
But there are major questions surrounding the development of a lunar lander, for which both SpaceX and Blue Origin have multibillion-dollar development contracts. Depending on how these projects go, a US lunar landing could be delayed to 2030 or even later.
Although it is virtually impossible for outsiders to glean information about technical milestones achieved inside China’s space program, the country is clearly making credible progress toward reaching the Moon. For example, in August 2025, the China Manned Space Agency successfully tested a high-fidelity mock-up of its 26-ton Lanyue lunar lander. The test used giant tethers to simulate lunar gravity as the vehicle fired its main engines and fine-control thrusters to land on a cratered surface and take off from a location near Beijing.
Recently, the Mengzhou spacecraft for the 2027 test atop a Long March 10A rocket arrived at the Wenchang Space Launch Site in Hainan, China, where the mission will launch.
US government assessments of the Chinese space program are restricted, but lawmakers are clearly taking the threat seriously. In the last 12 months, the US Congress and White House have given broad latitude to NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman to streamline the Artemis Program to land humans on the Moon. He has moved swiftly to cancel the Lunar Gateway space station and planned upgrades to the Space Launch System rocket. And just last week, Isaacman announced plans to help Blue Origin develop a lunar lander by finding a way to boost the Orion spacecraft into low-lunar orbit.
“We have the mandate, we have the resources, and the support from our stakeholders to be able to execute, and that’s what we intend to do,” he said at the time.
For a couple of years, it has been clear that China has made a major commitment to landing astronauts on the Moon, preferably before the United States returns to the lunar surface, to score a major geopolitical win. Beyond this near-term competition, both NASA and China’s space program are building capabilities to establish a long-term presence at the Moon’s South Pole. As part of this second phase of the contest, Isaacman committed NASA to the development of a base on the surface of the Moon over the next decade.

articles.title_orig: Google rolling out gradient icon redesigns for Contacts, Messages, and Phone
articles.title_zh: Google rolling out gradient icon redesigns for Contacts, Messages, and Phone
articles.content_orig:
Following the Workspace and Pixel app redesigns earlier this year, Google is overhauling the Contacts, Messages, and Phone icons.
Google says the “icons are sharper and clearer” on homescreens thanks to a “subtle but crisp gradient with easily readable edges.”
These are less visually cluttered than the old ones with the intersecting lines and hints of layering. They weren't bad but I like these a lot better.
The general shapes of Google’s communication apps remain unchanged, but the redesign brings “updated curvature and coloring to align with the rest of the Google apps you know and love.”
This change is rolling out over the coming weeks via the Play Store, and is already live with the latest Google Messages beta this morning. Google emphasizes that there are no functional changes with this update.
Don’t worry, the functionality of these apps isn’t changing as a result of the new icons. You’ll simply spot a sleeker, more cohesive look on your home screen in the coming weeks.
The new icons should also appear on contacts.google.com and messages.google.com/web.

articles.title_orig: Apple’s ‘Ultra’ smart home robot might have to wait until 2028
articles.title_zh: Apple’s ‘Ultra’ smart home robot might have to wait until 2028
articles.content_orig:
The HomeView-like tabletop robot could cost over $1,000, reports The Information.﻿
The HomeView-like tabletop robot could cost over $1,000, reports The Information.﻿
Apple has reportedly delayed the launch of its rumored smart home robot until next year at the earliest or possibly even 2028, according to The Information . It says the robot’s hardware “has been finished for around two years,” but that the software isn’t ready. The device’s software team has reportedly pushed to delay the launch and “attempted to strip back some proposed features and focus the product on a few capabilities related to FaceTime and automating home tasks, like switching on a light.”
According to The Information , the device is codenamed J595, but former Apple employees predict it will be called the “HomeView Ultra,” taking after the new HomeView smart display that launched last month. The robot might cost significantly more than the HomeView, though, at around $1,000, potentially more depending on price hikes for RAM and other components.
Bloomberg ’s Mark Gurman said in 2024 that the robot could have a stationary, tabletop design resembling Pixar’s famous lamp . The Information says it will have a 9-inch display that swivels around on a robotic arm, with cameras and sensors for things like following you around during a FaceTime call.

articles.title_orig: Squarespace is laying off 19 percent of employees
articles.title_zh: Squarespace is laying off 19 percent of employees
articles.content_orig:
The layoffs will impact about 300 workers.
The layoffs will impact about 300 workers.
The website-building platform Squarespace is laying off 19 percent of its employees as it works to “simplify” its operations, Squarespace spokesperson Jeff Seedman says in a statement to The Verge . The job cuts will affect around 300 of Squarespace’s 1,800 employees .
“The changes are intended to simplify how we operate, sharpen our priorities and enable the company to move faster as we position Squarespace for its next phase of growth,” Seedman says. “We are grateful for the contributions of our departing colleagues and are providing comprehensive support to help them through the transition.” Seedman adds that impacted employees will receive 16 weeks of base pay and healthcare benefits into May 2027.
The layoffs come a little over two years after Squarespace’s big push into AI. In 2024, the company announced its Blueprint AI tool , which uses AI to build websites as well as generate website copy, blog posts, product descriptions, and more. The private equity firm Permira also closed its acquisition of Squarespace around that time.

articles.title_orig: Why Orban and Vucic Broke With Trump on Election Denial
articles.title_zh: Why Orban and Vucic Broke With Trump on Election Denial
articles.content_orig:
Rep. Adam Smith, a Washington Democrat who has served in the House since 1996, at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 4, 2025.
When the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee was asked by TIME in May about the prospect of impeaching President Donald Trump, he declined to commit, warning that every impeachment he had witnessed during his decades in Congress had left its target politically stronger. Five months later, Rep. Adam Smith of Washington is prepared to take that risk.
With Democrats hoping to reclaim control of the House in Tuesday's midterm elections, Smith says that he now supports impeaching Trump and is inclined to also back proceedings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , making him one of the most senior Democrats to endorse such a course.
"Trump has become beyond dangerous. He is just completely out of control in what he says and how he is governing," Smith told TIME in an interview a week before the election. "I think we have to try, even if it doesn't succeed."
Smith's endorsement is particularly significant because he would be in line to chair the Armed Services Committee if Democrats win the House, putting him at the center of investigations into the Pentagon's handling of the war with Iran, its approach to Ukraine, and military operations in Latin America.
His position comes as Democrats prepare for the possibility of reclaiming congressional power with little agreement over how aggressively to confront the President. Interviews with more than two dozen Democrats reveal a party broadly convinced that Trump has engaged in conduct warranting impeachment, but deeply divided over whether another attempt to remove him would be an effective use of its authority. Trump's two previous impeachments ended in Senate acquittals, and even a Democratic victory this week is unlikely to produce anything approaching the two-thirds majority required for conviction.
Read more: Calls to Impeach Trump Collide With Reluctant Democratic Leadership
Smith, who has served in the House since 1996, noted previously that he was one of the few House members to have sat through three impeachments. "Every single time the person impeached got stronger after they were impeached than before," Smith told TIME in May, arguing that Democrats needed to consider what another impeachment could realistically achieve rather than pursue it simply to demonstrate their willingness to confront Trump. "I want to make sure that if we're going down that road it's going to help defeat Trump and his poisonous ideology," he said at the time.
Since then, he says, Trump's increasingly conciliatory posture toward Russian President Vladimir Putin, his decisions involving American support for Ukraine, and his public rhetoric have convinced him that the President's continued tenure presents an extraordinary danger. "The Ukraine stuff definitely had a profound impact," Smith says. "When I saw how close he was getting to Putin and shutting off support for Ukraine, being more pro-Putin. I mean, that's a big part of it." He also cites Trump's increasingly "unhinged speeches," including remarks about rising gasoline prices amid the war in the Middle East.
Smith’s willingness to embrace impeachment puts him at odds with more cautious Democrats who want the party to prioritize addressing the economic concerns that have dominated the campaign, while establishing an investigative record that might ultimately lead to impeachment. He acknowledges the formidable obstacles to removing Trump but argues that the political environment has changed since the President's first term. "I don't think it will be viewed as negatively or as partisan as in the previous two efforts, just because the public is waking up to the con game that Trump put on," he says now. "The impeachable offenses have been obvious for a long time.”
Other senior House Democrats are less certain that pursuing impeachment would accomplish much, even if they share Smith's assessment of Trump's conduct. Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who led the House managers during Trump's second impeachment trial in 2021, says he has "little doubt that the president has committed multiple impeachable offenses," citing what he describes as unconstitutional military action and abuses of congressional spending authority. But he draws a distinction between establishing grounds for impeachment and deciding whether another trial would be the best use of Congress's time and political capital.
"The question of whether he committed impeachable offenses and whether we are going to pursue impeachment are two different issues," Raskin tells TIME.
Trump was impeached in 2019 over his dealings with Ukraine and again in 2021 over his role in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. Both proceedings ended in acquittal, although seven Republican senators voted to convict him in the second trial. While some Democrats regarded those efforts as necessary to establish a historical and constitutional record, another impeachment could consume months of congressional attention, galvanize Trump's supporters, and leave voters questioning what the party had accomplished with its new majority.
Sen. Adam Schiff of California, who led the prosecution during Trump's first impeachment trial, says Democrats should avoid reaching conclusions before knowing the composition of the next Congress and what investigations might uncover. "There's no question he's been engaging in conduct that is very likely impeachable," Schiff told TIME. "The question is, is it viable?"
Schiff disputes the notion that the earlier impeachment efforts strengthened Trump politically, but argues that Democrats should concentrate initially on investigating corruption that has affected Americans' finances. "Our primary focus ought to be on corruption that has raised the cost of living for people," he says.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has similarly declined to commit to impeachment, saying Democrats "haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out." He has indicated that investigations should help determine whether the House pursues that course.
Some Democrats are looking toward members of Trump's Cabinet, particularly Hegseth, as potentially more viable targets, reasoning that Republicans who would never vote to remove the President might be more willing to turn against a defense secretary whose leadership has drawn criticism from within their own party. "There are Republicans who would support impeaching Hegseth who might not support doing it to Trump," Smith says.
The Defense Secretary has faced mounting scrutiny over his handling of the Iran war, the removal of senior military officers, and the Pentagon's relationship with Congress. Some Republicans have publicly expressed frustration with his leadership and the department's failure to provide adequate information about the war's objectives, costs, and duration. A push to impeach him has already taken shape in the Republican-controlled House, although Trump has defended Hegseth, calling him a "great warrior" and dismissing Democratic efforts to remove him.
Raskin says that impeaching a Cabinet secretary would be less likely to consume Congress's agenda or raise the same concerns about overturning the result of a presidential election. "The question of cabinet officers is a little bit easier because it doesn't necessarily consume all of the policy oxygen in Congress," he says.
However, impeaching Hegseth would require a majority in the House, and removing him would still require a two-thirds vote in the Senate. Republicans who have criticized his performance have not necessarily indicated any willingness to support impeachment. But the growing unease over the administration's military decisions, particularly the conduct and costs of the war with Iran, could offer Democrats an opening that does not exist with Trump.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX reportedly wants to buy Boost Mobile to compete with AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
articles.title_zh: SpaceX reportedly wants to buy Boost Mobile to compete with AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.
SpaceX is looking to buy Boost Mobile from EchoStar, according to a report from The Washington Post. If the deal goes through, it would help the Elon Musk-owned company build a hybrid cellular-satellite network that could help catapult it into fourth place among the top U.S. wireless providers.
The space-launch company has been dabbling in cellular connectivity, rolling out satellite access to T-Mobile’s subscribers in 2024. Last year, SpaceX bought $17 billion worth of wireless spectrum from EchoStar for cellular services, which could help the company’s Starlink service reach inside buildings, for example, something it currently struggles with.
“This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America,” Musk said on X at the time of the spectrum acquisition. Yet, if Musk is still looking to buy access to terrestrial networks, it apparently wasn’t the last piece.
Elon Musk, SpaceX’s CEO, reportedly spoke directly with EchoStar chairman Charlie Ergen in October about acquiring Boost Mobile, the mobile virtual network operator. EchoStar has about 7.5 million customers between Boost Mobile and GenMobile, its other mobile service offering.
Musk has also approached AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon about buying capacity on their networks. All three rejected Musk, and they may still have a say in a SpaceX acquisition of Boost Mobile. Boost doesn’t operate its own towers, instead leasing capacity from AT&T and T-Mobile, which might need to approve such a deal. Sources speaking to The Post said that network leases are usually nontransferable.
The big three providers each have over 100 million subscribers, dwarfing Boost Mobile. But while the acquisition would give SpaceX an immediate bump in subscribers, the true value of the deal would be giving the company access to terrestrial cellular networks.
Gaining access to towers leased to Boost Mobile would expand coverage significantly — Boost currently covers most of the 48 contiguous states in the U.S. — allowing Starlink to cover devices when they’re outdoors and relying on cell towers to handle devices when Starlink signals can’t reach them.

articles.title_orig: Privacy Display on Galaxy S27 Pro and S27 Ultra looks more promising in latest leak
articles.title_zh: Privacy Display on Galaxy S27 Pro and S27 Ultra looks more promising in latest leak
articles.content_orig:
A new leak strengthens a previous rumor that the Galaxy S27 Pro and Galaxy S27 Ultra will get an improved version of Samsung’s Privacy Display, used on this year’s flagship.
We don’t expect Samsung to just walk away from the Privacy Display feature. It’s a cool addition that’s over-the-top on the surface, but proves useful in certain situations, like localized notification dimming so only the user can see their messages.
The latest leak regarding Samsung’s component options for the Galaxy S27 series indicates two devices in the next Galaxy S series will get a Privacy Display, or at least some version of it. The leak claims the Galaxy S27 Pro and Galaxy S27 Ultra’s Privacy Display will have “enhanced display brightness.”
That’s the only new detail after the display choice was leaked in September . Both leaks claim the same details – only the upper two models will have a display capable of blocking views from certain angles. The Galaxy S27 and Galaxy S27 Plus won’t be so lucky. It makes some sense considering the Galaxy S27 Pro may essentially take the place of the current Ultra.
There are few details beyond the display’s brightness capabilities. One would hope Samsung improves on overall quality, so using the feature doesn’t have to come with many trade-offs.
Samsung is expected to launch the Galaxy S27 series early next year, though no date has been nailed down.

articles.title_orig: Nearly Two Thousand Chinese Businesses Established in Nicaragua Since Free Trade Agreement Took Effect
articles.title_zh: Nearly Two Thousand Chinese Businesses Established in Nicaragua Since Free Trade Agreement Took Effect
articles.content_orig:
COSTA RICA'S LEADING ENGLISH LANGUAGE NEWSPAPER
Nearly 2,000 Chinese businesses have been established in Nicaragua during the first two years of the free trade agreement with China, according to the president of the Asociación Pro-Unificación Pacífica de China en Nicaragua. Shujin Huang made the statement to official media outlets after an event marking the 160th anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen.
He said the association continues to promote additional investment from China, describing Nicaragua as a safe country with a competitive market. The free trade agreement between the two countries entered into force on January 1, 2024. The Banco Central de Nicaragua reported that net foreign direct investment from China reached 29.3 million dollars in 2025.
That figure represented 1.9 percent of the 1,502.5 million dollars in total net foreign direct investment recorded by the country that year. In 2024, any Chinese flows were not reported separately and would have been included in aggregate categories if present at all. Huang said the businesses operate mainly in commerce, with some also active in free-zone maquilas. The relatively low official investment total relative to the number of establishments indicates that most are small-scale operations.
The Asociación Pro-Unificación Pacífica de China en Nicaragua was founded in May 2024 and was officially registered as a legal organization under Ministerial Agreement 24-2024-OSFL, allowing it to operate in its own name under Nicaraguan law. Its founding event included participation by Chinese Ambassador Chen Xi and Nicaraguan officials including National Assembly President Gustavo Porras, Foreign Minister Denis Moncada and Presidential Adviser Laureano Ortega Murillo.
As part of the commercial expansion, construction of a Chinatown complex advances in Managua near the Rotonda Universitaria. The project, also known as Plaza China or Plaza 101, involves a two-story structure of approximately 8,000 square meters with an investment of about 3 million dollars. It is planned to house around 100 businesses operated by Chinese, other Asian and Nicaraguan owners.
The site currently holds roughly 30 businesses. Administrators have described the work as being in an intermediate phase, including installation of a stone arch more than six meters high carved in a dragon style and brought from China. The complex is intended to concentrate commercial activity, gastronomy and cultural offerings. Huang cited the existing Plaza China as an example of growing Chinese capital presence, noting that more than ten foreign-investment businesses already operate there.
Nicaragua and China restored diplomatic relations in December 2021 after Managua broke ties with Taiwan. The free trade agreement was signed on August 31, 2023. Official Nicaraguan statements have presented the pact and related initiatives as measures to expand trade and investment opportunities. The association’s stated goals include supporting Chinese investors and promoting the policy of one China.
As of now, the association continues to encourage further arrivals of Chinese capital. Construction on the Managua Chinatown project remains under way, with officials and association representatives describing it as a visible marker of the commercial presence that has developed since the trade agreement took effect. The Banco Central de Nicaragua has not published a full country-by-country breakdown beyond the 2025 net total that places China at 29.3 million dollars.

articles.title_orig: Labour to end power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
articles.title_zh: Labour to end power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
articles.content_orig:
The Labour Party has pulled out of power-sharing agreements with the Green Party in 11 local councils, after the national party adopted a policy defining Zionism as a form of racism.
Labour councillors will no longer be in coalition with the Greens in areas including Sheffield, Warwick and Lewes.
Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said: "Labour has been clear from the start that the "Zionism is Racism" policy crosses a line and we cannot work with any party that supports it – at any level of government."
Green leader Zack Polanski said the move would "backfire" on Labour and accused the party of wanting to "interrupt your local services and impose genocide support from it's local councils".
In October, Green Party members backed a motion, entitled "Zionism is racism", which said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish State in historic Palestine". Israel has denied committing genocide in Gaza.
The motion also backed a "single democratic Palestinian State", including in modern-day Israel.
Having been backed by party members, the motion became Green Party policy, but it has left senior figures bitterly divided . Jewish groups and opposition political parties have condemned it.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs in October that Labour would not partner with the Greens over the "antisemitic" policy.
Labour then issued an ultimatum from Labour's head office to Labour-Green councils, demanding that local Greens disown the motion passed by members at their national party conference.
Green groups were also asked to call on their party's national leadership to reconsider the policy.
Labour said there were local agreements in place in 18 authorities. Of those, Labour said 11 had not met the criteria it demanded.
Labour said its conditions had been met in Broadland, Monmouthshire, North Somerset, Rother, West Oxfordshire and West Sussex. The party said that Coventry City Council does not have a formal arrangement in place and that no such deal will be made in the future.
It will continue co-operating with the Greens in the West of England mayoralty, where the deputy mayor is a Green member.
Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said the motion was "imperfect" but has defended its central premise , arguing that Israel's actions towards the Palestinian people are "clearly underpinned by racist ideology".
The collapse of co-operation at the local level could impact hundreds of thousands of residents through budgets and policy decisions taking longer to get voted through.
Green and Labour councillors in the impacted areas will now have to seek alternative coalition partners or try to govern as a minority administration.
In a joint statement, the Green Party and the Local Government Association Green Group said it was "hugely disappointed" that Labour had forced local leaders into "jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents".
One of the biggest councils to be affected is Sheffield, where 25 Labour councillors formed a power-sharing agreement with 20 Green councillors after the May 2026 elections for the Yorkshire city's 550,000 residents.
Responding to Labour's ultimatum, leader of the Sheffield Greens Angela Argenzio did not mention the motion in a letter but insisted local Green councillors "are not antisemitic".
Argenzio told local Labour representatives they were being "directed by your national party leader" rather than local concerns.
In a statement on Monday, the council's Labour leader Cllr Fran Belbin said her party would propose on Wednesday that it proceeds as a Labour minority administration.
"We now feel we are at the end of the road with the joint administration," she said.
"Our trust in Sheffield Greens is completely broken," she added, accusing them of a "refusal to stand up for Jewish citizens".
Green Party co-deputy leader Rachel Millward, also the leader of Wealden Council, said: "It is ironic that a Labour prime minister who made a promise to solve problems, not score points, has now shown he is willing to disrupt well-run councils for fear of Green success."
She added: "It is utterly irresponsible to conflate criticism of the actions of the state of Israel with antisemitism. Many Jewish people strongly reject the illegal actions of the current Israeli government."
In Warwick, the local Green party said: "We refuse to condemn a democratically decided policy because of political intimidation."
It urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to "reflect his own words in his actions and allow local Labour groups to decide for themselves".
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Green group leader in Havant Netty Shepherd accused Labour of "performative politics" and said the end of their coalition would be a "complete disaster for residents".
"I am a local government councillor, I worry about people's bins, I worry about generating town centres - foreign policy is nothing to do with my remit," she added.
The Liberal Democrats are also in partnership with the Green Party in some local councils.
Last week, the party leader Sir Ed Davey ruled out entering into a national partnership with "any party that is committed to a dangerous and antisemitic policy like the Green Party's".
He added that he had asked those of his local leaders in coalition with the Greens to urge Green councillors to reject the motion and commit to campaigning for its reversal.

articles.title_orig: Leicestershire Reform council leader quits after staff comments leaked
articles.title_zh: Leicestershire Reform council leader quits after staff comments leaked
articles.content_orig:
The Reform UK leader of Leicestershire County Council has announced he is standing down after comments he made about staff redundancies were leaked online.
Dan Harrison announced on Monday that he would be stepping down from the role he has held since May 2025.
He said he had made the decision after taking advice from senior Reform colleagues, and added deputy council leader Kevin Crook had taken over as acting leader.
It comes after Harrison had apologised after being recorded saying 76 council solicitors would be made redundant, branding them "incompetent", before saying "what I want to look at now is the women", in remarks which were then released on social media.
In a statement, Harrison said it had been the "honour of his life" to lead the county council's first Reform administration.
Harrison has said he will remain as a councillor, representing the Ashby-de-la-Zouch division.
The Conservative opposition at County Hall had called for Harrison to resign after his comments about staff were leaked.
In the recording, Harrison said: "There's 76 solicitors will be made redundant.
"We'll buy in the service, because [they are] incompetent. They're not doing a good job.
"What I want to look at now is the women so it is ongoing, I would like it to be at great pace but I can tell you now if we suddenly drove massive redundancies the liberals would walk away."
Earlier on Monday, Harrison had told the BBC he would not be stepping down - but he later said he made his decision after talking to Crook and group whip Andrew Hamilton-Gray.
He had apologised over the remarks, which were made on Tuesday during a Reform party meeting.
Despite his apology, Harrison had insisted his remarks had been taken out of context.
Harrison said: "I would like to apologise unreservedly to the staff and officers of the county council for any hurt, distress or offence caused by the publication of these comments, which were made during a heated meeting with the expectation of privacy and confidentiality.
"However, I would like to stress that these discussions were just that, and I have not given any instruction or direction to officers in these matters and that there has not been any discussion nor agreement on these issues with officers."
He added: "I unequivocally reject any suggestion that staffing decisions are being taken based on gender.
"The comments made in that meeting were taken completely out of context."
Before Harrison's resignation, the council's 15 Tory councillors had called for an emergency vote to try to remove him from the leader's role.
Group leader of the Conservative group, Deborah Taylor, said: "That was not a decision we took lightly.
"The serious concerns raised over recent days, particularly around the treatment of council employees and the comments contained in leaked recordings, left us feeling that his position had become untenable.
"His resignation brings an end to his leadership, but it does not mean those concerns should simply be forgotten.
"There are still questions that deserve answers, and it is important that the council learns from what has happened."
The Reform group remains the largest party on the authority, and runs it as a minority administration.
In a statement, Jeevun Sandher and Amanda Hack - Labour MPs for Loughborough and North West Leicestershire respectively - said: "Since taking office in 2025, the Reform UK administration has become increasingly embroiled in controversy and scandal, rather than focusing on delivering for the residents of Leicestershire.
"This is far from an isolated incident. Just last week, councillor [Joseph] Boam was found to have breached the council's own code of conduct through his actions against the former monitoring officer, while other Reform councillors have also been forced to apologise to residents over their behaviour. All of this in less than two years.
"Leicestershire residents deserve better."

articles.title_orig: Can Pakistan Help Break China’s Critical Minerals Dominance?
articles.title_zh: Can Pakistan Help Break China’s Critical Minerals Dominance?
articles.content_orig:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks with Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir before meeting with President Donald Trump in the Oval Office, on September 25, 2025. Pakistan’s  mineral wealth can help break China’s hold on the global critical minerals market, writes Derek Grossman. (The White House/Daniel Torok)
China has spent decades building a near-stranglehold on critical mineral supply chains, leaving the United States dangerously dependent on its chief strategic rival. Even President Donald Trump ’s recent trade truce with Chinese leader Xi Jinping has done little to resolve the underlying problem: America’s continued dependence on Chinese processing of minerals essential to its economy and national security. But the Trump administration is aggressively challenging Beijing’s dominance across the globe, and over the past year, it has engaged an unlikely partner: Pakistan .
To be sure, Pakistan has been an important, if at times complicated, American strategic partner since the Cold War, helping Washington counter Soviet expansionism and, after the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, supporting US military operations in Afghanistan . Bilateral ties have seen periods of strain, but Trump’s return to the White House has brought a major reboot. Since then, Trump has met multiple times with senior Pakistani leaders, including Field Marshal Asim Munir and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. Most recently, Islamabad has served as a key mediator between the United States and Iran in efforts to end their war, ushering in a remarkable revival in bilateral relations.
And now, there’s apparently a new area to explore: critical minerals. Over the past year, the Trump administration has stepped up discussions with Islamabad on developing Pakistan’s largely untapped mineral wealth, including a $500 million agreement between an American company and Pakistan’s Frontier Works Organization to cooperate on mining and processing critical minerals, including rare earths.
Washington has also backed the massive Reko Diq copper and gold project through $1.25 billion in Export-Import Bank financing , underscoring its growing interest in Pakistan as an alternative source of strategic minerals. Pakistan, meanwhile, stands to benefit economically from greater American investment in a mining sector that currently accounts for only about 3 percent of its GDP.
Last April, a US delegation led by Eric Meyer of the State Department attended the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum in Islamabad and conveyed the interest of American companies in the sector. With the forum returning November 12–13 , renewed American participation—particularly if accompanied by fresh investment commitments—would demonstrate that Washington is serious about turning its growing interest in Pakistan’s mineral wealth into a lasting strategic partnership.
Deeper US-Pakistan cooperation on critical minerals could help Washington chip away at Beijing’s dominance over global supply chains. Early American investment could also help determine where Pakistan’s minerals are processed and who ultimately purchases them, rather than allowing Beijing to lock in these arrangements before Washington has a chance to compete.
Indeed, Pakistan is just one piece of the Trump administration’s broader strategy to reduce dependence on China, with Washington pursuing critical minerals agreements and partnerships across Asia, including Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Australia, as well as resource-rich countries such as Argentina, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Ukraine.
Washington’s experience in Africa suggests the bet can pay off. The Democratic Republic of the Congo is a country where conflict in the east has complicated the operating environment and where Chinese firms have long held the advantage, yet the United States has leaned in anyway, building on a Lobito Corridor initiative that began under the Biden administration and that Trump has carried forward. In December 2025, Washington and Kinshasa signed a Strategic Partnership Agreement reportedly giving American companies a right of first offer on designated mineral deposits.
This July, the Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa closed a $753 million package to upgrade the Lobito Atlantic Railway, which carries Congolese and Zambian copper and cobalt to Angola’s Atlantic coast, and the operator now expects to double its international cargo to 800,000 tons next year .
In May, the DRC’s state cobalt entity also agreed to supply cobalt hydroxide to a US-based firm. Progress has not been linear, and the DRC’s task force for the minerals pact was set up months behind schedule, but the lesson is clear: sustained commitment in a difficult jurisdiction can reshape supply chains in ways that waiting for ideal conditions never will. Pakistan has its own challenges, but trust built through early investment is what gives American companies a seat at the table.
But challenges remain. For starters, Pakistan’s evolving domestic security situation, particularly in mineral-rich Balochistan, will shape how quickly American companies can establish an on-the-ground presence. The Barrick Mining Corporation has slowed development of the massive Reko Diq copper and gold project while it reviews the security environment in Pakistan and the wider region, though it has said it continues to believe in the project’s long-term value and has kept Phase 1 approved, a reminder that investors will need to price in risk and that Islamabad has a strong interest in improving the conditions for them.
Another constraint is that Beijing, having entered Pakistan’s mining sector much earlier, already enjoys significant advantages in infrastructure, expertise, and established commercial relationships, forcing Washington to play catch-up. According to a recent Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) report, China already purchases approximately 95 percent of Pakistan’s exported copper ores and concentrates, illustrating just how deeply Beijing is embedded in Pakistan’s existing minerals trade.
Nevertheless, the upcoming critical minerals conference, along with potential new Trump administration agreements with Islamabad, could help narrow this gap—provided they translate into concrete investments and sustained cooperation. Moreover, much of Pakistan’s critical mineral wealth remains underexplored, giving American companies a chance to help identify and develop commercially viable deposits, particularly antimony—a strategically important critical mineral used in ammunition, explosives, flame retardants, and advanced military technologies, making it essential to US defense manufacturing and national security—while potentially establishing new processing facilities outside China’s control. Islamabad also has an incentive to welcome American investment as a way to diversify its economic relationships without abandoning its longstanding strategic partnership with Beijing.
Though making that case a reality will take more than just this. Washington could start by pairing its financing with tools that help American firms manage the risks of a frontier jurisdiction, such as political risk insurance and co-financing alongside development banks and Gulf investors, so that capital can move before conditions are perfect. It should prioritize processing as much as extraction, because the real leverage lies in refining, and the opportunity to build facilities outside China’s control is greatest while Pakistan’s sector is still taking shape.
And it should treat the relationship as a durable economic partnership rather than an extension of its diplomacy around Iran, with offtake agreements and technical cooperation that give both sides a stake in the outcome.
