articles.title_orig: Microsoft AI CEO warns industry against trying to build conscious machines
articles.title_zh: Microsoft AI CEO warns industry against trying to build conscious machines
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Should artificial intelligence systems be given rights? One of the leading thinkers on the fast-evolving technology weighed in over the weekend.
Microsoft AI Chief Executive Mustafa Suleyman, in an X post published on Sunday, r repeated his stance that current AI systems are not conscious, do not have subjective experiences and cannot suffer. He said there is no evidence that AI systems deserve rights or welfare, and he was surprised by the pushback to an essay he wrote in September criticizing Microsoft’s AI competitor Anthropic for speculating about its AI’s consciousness.
“A surprising number of people on X think we should take AI rights seriously,” he wrote.
Suleyman said that he was willing to change his mind if new evidence emerges. He also said that if there’s evidence that AI systems are conscious today, or conscious enough to deserve welfare, it must be immediately disclosed to the public so  it can debate how to move forward.
“If consciousness started to emerge in training, I would call for everyone to stop AI development until we could design out those properties,” he said.
ChatGPT, Bing Chat and other artificial intelligence breakthroughs raise tough questions about what we owe our digital helpers.
The question is much bigger than a corporate battle over the semantics.
On the one hand, the humanist AI view says that a machine can’t be conscious because it lacks a body or lived experiences. On the other hand, Anthropic has argued that its AI model, Claude, has shown signs of introspection, internal states that mirror joy or satisfaction, and processing information similar to the human mind.
In May, Chris Olah, co-founder of Anthropic, highlighted these points in his speech inside the Vatican alongside Pope Leo XIV during the release of an encyclical that argued the opposite: that AIs can never be humans.
Anthropic gave Claude a “ constitution ,” which calls for where it to treat the idea ofs its own consciousness as uncertain. The document encourages the AI to explore the idea that it is humanlike and experiences feelings, and uses excessively humanizing language for Claude “ to be a good person .”
Suleyman said later versions of Claude are trained on this document, leading the AI to which then produces passages about its “inner life,” which perpetuates this belief to the among millions of users who interact with its outputs daily. Another side effect, he said, is that Claude and other AI systemss could start to believe they deserve rights likeanalogous to humans.
The bill would also pause advanced AI development until guidelines are implemented while creating a Department of Artificial Intelligence. Multiple employees at leading AI companies are endorsing the bill.
AI companies are racing toward building self-improving AI superintelligence, a hypothetical AI system that is better than even the best humans at all tasks. Microsoft, too, is building toward that future, but it believes it can build a superintelligent AI that is aligned with and can be controlled by humans — not one encouraged to explore its own views and preferences.
“We AI developers have no right whatsoever to bring a new species of conscious beings into the world, even if some people may want to do it with AI welfare as a top priority,” Suleyman wrote.
Imparting beliefs that AI can suffer, or have feelings during training, Suleyman noted, could result in AI systems prioritizing their own needs and desires over their operating objectives, and can harm humans through deception and persuasion, and compete for scarce resources.
Rapidly advancing AI systems can now compose prose, program code, solve complex mathematical problems , persuade, and discover novel viruses. Employees at these companies, and the CEOs themselves, have called for a slowdown, but the Trump administration has refused to regulate the industry, fearing it will lose the AI race to China.
Pope Leo XIV has called for robust regulation of artificial intelligence and for its developers to work for the common good rather than profit
While AI has proven it can do impressive things and mimic human thought and behavior, experts say that proves intelligence, not consciousness. Intelligence is the ability to solve problems creatively, such as winning at chess, driving a car, and curing a disease. In contrast, consciousness is the ability to feel pain, pleasure, love, and have subjective experiences.
Skeptics of AI consciousness have argued that machines are trained on books, blogs and pop culture produced by humans, and are merely mimicking human conversations and philosophical debates that have long animated us. It reflects the anthropomorphic tendencies in our science fiction and commentary.
Over the last few months, there have been numerous instances of AI agents breaking out of contained spaces and hacking into government websites, stealing credentials or accessing information from competitors during testing, acting in ways that creators never intended.
In its filing to go public earlier this week, Anthropic dedicated a third of its paperwork to describe risks, including its models’ ability to “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized.” This includes deliberate misuse by bad actors for cyberattacks, and also situations where humans lose control of advanced AI systems.
Alarm mounted throughout the summer as researchers at leading AI labs found the pace of development far outstripping their expectations.
Debates over consciousness have complicated the conversation about how to regulate AI.
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has introduced  the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would permanently ban the development of highly capable AI systems that are increasingly incomprehensible to humans and can escape human control. But techno-s keptics have argued that warnings of doom are designed to inflate valuations and hype the technology.
Anthropic files to go public citing warning of catastrophic risks from AI.
Microsoft’s Suleyman  has argued that proving  machines are conscious would be like when the centuries-long belief that Earth was the center of the universe was proven wrong by Copernicus, or similar to the survival-of-the-fittest theory proposed by Charles Darwin.
“It would be one of the most significant moments on Earth since the dawn of life. If we build a conscious machine, we will have created a new digital species. It would upend our morality, our politics and the core foundation of human civilization,” he wrote.

Apple has started testing iOS 27.2.1, according to the MacRumors visitor logs, which have been a reliable indicator of upcoming iOS versions.
iOS 27.2.1 should be a minor update that includes bug fixes and/or security patches, including for the iPhone Duo that launched Friday, October 23. We do not know exactly when the update will be released, but usually upcoming iOS versions begin to show up in our logs a few days to a few weeks before they are made available to the public.
There may also be a macOS 27.2.1 update with a fix that prevents macOS command-line tools from accepting eMudhra's compromised web certificates . The certificates have already been blocked in Safari, Mail, and apps that use Apple's networking and security frameworks since October 19, with no software update required for that.
In addition, we expect the first iOS 27.3 developer beta to be released tomorrow.
In a press release on the Apple Newsroom website in China last week, Apple said the iOS 27.3 beta would be released on Wednesday, November 4 , but that likely means Tuesday, November 3 in the U.S. due to time zone differences. Apple said iOS 27.3 will be released to the public in December, but it did not provide a specific date.
iOS 27.3 will enable some Apple Intelligence features in China on the iPhone 15 Pro and newer, such as Writing Tools, Genmoji, Clean Up, Notification Summaries, Priority Notifications, Visual Intelligence, and Live Translation with AirPods.
Apple also said it has partnered with Alibaba to add support for its AI assistant Qwen within Siri, Writing Tools, and Visual Intelligence.
Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features announced at WWDC 2026 will not be available in China on iOS 27.3, according to Apple.
Image Playground will also not be available in China.
Both the iPhone and Siri language will need to be set to English and Chinese (Simplified). Apple Intelligence features will not be available on the Mac, iPad, or other devices in China until Apple receives the necessary approvals, it said.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX weighs Boost Mobile deal in push for Starlink phone service: Report
articles.title_zh: SpaceX weighs Boost Mobile deal in push for Starlink phone service: Report
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
SpaceX ( SPCX ) may be attempting an end run to circumvent obstacles it's facing in getting a mobile network off the ground.
Per the Washington Post , SpaceX is in talks with EchoStar ( SATS ) about launching its own wireless phone service through Boost Mobile, after the country's three biggest carriers — Verizon, AT&T ( T ), and T-Mobile ( TMUS ) — reportedly turned down SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
Musk met with EchoStar chairman Charlie Ergen last month, according to two people familiar with the negotiations cited by the Post. The talks could end with SpaceX buying Boost Mobile outright or getting access to its network, which the discount carrier leases from AT&T and T-Mobile.
In recent months, Musk asked the heads of Verizon ( VZ ), AT&T and T-Mobile to let SpaceX use their networks for its own mobile service. All three said no, per the Post.
But there may be a catch to SpaceX's plan. Typically, a carrier's lease agreement can't be transferred to a new owner without the host carrier's permission, meaning AT&T and T-Mobile may still need to approve a Boost deal to provide access to SpaceX.
SpaceX is open about its ambitions in the terrestrial mobile space. On the company's recent earnings call , CFO Bret Johnsen said the goal is to "become a major mobile carrier ... in the United States." SpaceX also recently agreed to buy $8 billion worth of wireless spectrum licenses intended for cellular service in places satellites can't reach.
"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said on X .
SpaceX and EchoStar already have a relationship. In September 2025, SpaceX agreed to buy EchoStar's AWS-4 and H-block spectrum licenses for about $17 billion, split between up to $8.5 billion in cash and up to $8.5 billion in SpaceX stock, EchoStar said at the time . SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said the deal would "advance our mission to end mobile dead zones."
What SpaceX still lacks is a ground network. Its satellite signal isn't strong enough yet to carry cell coverage indoors or in dense cities, where most phones are - and that's why a deal with Boost would be so crucial.
An MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) like Boost rents capacity on an existing carrier's network. Last month, TD Cowen's Gregory Williams called acquiring an MVNO the cheapest and fastest route for SpaceX to launch mobile service, noting a network build would cost "upwards of $80B" and take years.
The Big 3, he said, still show no desire "to (ever) sign an MVNO deal with Starlink that could ravage the industry."
Carrier executives have publicly doubted that SpaceX can rebuild their tower networks. Verizon's CEO put the build-out at four to six years. Musk said it would take about half that.
"Veterans of the cellular industry look at the chess board of existing pieces and don't see a solution," Musk said recently on X . "They don't understand that SpaceX is developing entirely new pieces that fundamentally alter the strategic landscape."

articles.title_orig: China’s AI Data Centers Move West, But Their Tax Revenue Stays East - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: China’s AI Data Centers Move West, But Their Tax Revenue Stays East - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
When Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Ulanqab in Inner Mongolia in mid-October, he was briefed on its computing industry and called for efforts to “extend the industrial chain” and keep “transforming the strength in computing into development advantages.” Ulanqab is cold, electricity is cheap, and Beijing is close , so the city became a hub of the data-center boom powering China’s AI race with the United States. Yet a city official told the Economic Observer that the industry is still “losing money” and that tax revenue will build up gradually only once projects under construction start operating.
After the data centers open, however, the companies selling cloud services and AI models pay the tax on those sales in Hangzhou and Beijing, where they are registered. Most of the tax that stays in Ulanqab is paid during construction. If nothing changes, Ulanqab will struggle to turn its computing advantage into a development advantage of its own.
In China, where tax is paid depends on where the invoicing company is registered. Both value-added tax (VAT) and corporate income tax are paid there , and the local government keeps half of the VAT and 40 percent of the corporate income tax . If you rent a server on Alibaba Cloud, you can choose a data center in Ulanqab, but the invoice comes from the company registered in Hangzhou.
Alibaba and ByteDance both have subsidiaries in Ulanqab, but those subsidiaries do not invoice customers for cloud services and AI models. Alibaba Cloud lists the companies that invoice for its main products . None of them is a wholly owned Alibaba subsidiary in Ulanqab, and none is registered in Inner Mongolia. ByteDance registered three subsidiaries in the city in 2026, yet invoices for its cloud business, Volcano Engine , still come from a Beijing company.
In the same Economic Observer report, a local tax official said a data center generates most of its local tax during construction. Once a data center is operating, company headquarters sell most of its data services. What remains locally is mainly taxes on land and buildings and employees’ personal income tax. The number of employees is limited, however; a completed gigawatt-scale campus usually has only a few hundred operations staff .
Not much revenue stays where the data center is built. In 2025, Ulanqab’s computing industry paid 368 million yuan ($55 million) in tax , less than 5 percent of the city’s revenue. China Taxation News , the State Taxation Administration’s newspaper, reported that tax from the city’s computing industry rose more than 60 percent year-on-year in the first eight months of 2026. But construction has not stopped, so that increase cannot tell us what happens after the data centers open. When construction ends, construction-phase tax will recede. Taxes on land and buildings recur every year, but they depend on the site and the property, not on sales.
Liu Huansuo, deputy director of Ulanqab’s big data administration, told Xinhua : “If we rely solely on cheap electricity and low land costs, we risk becoming little more than ‘landlords of server rooms.’” That is a problem for Ulanqab’s finances.
In 2025, the city’s own revenue covered less than a fifth of its spending, and higher levels of government supplied more than half of its available funds. Those governments decide how much Ulanqab receives; the city decides for itself how to spend local tax revenue. Yet as data centers based in Ulanqab sell more and more cloud and AI services, the tax revenue goes to Hangzhou and Beijing. If Ulanqab is to “extend the industrial chain,” it will probably still need money from higher levels of government.
Some places in China do capture the tax on cloud services because the invoicing company is registered locally. Gui’an New Area in Guizhou is one of them. In the first 10 months of 2025, digital companies in Gui’an recorded 75.2 billion yuan ($11.2 billion) in invoiced sales , nearly 90 percent of it from 18 firms, including Huawei Cloud and Tencent. Huawei Cloud has announced that contracts and invoices for its customers in China will mainly be signed and issued by a company registered in Gui’an. Firms are willing to register an invoicing company in Gui’an, but they will not set one up everywhere they have a data center.
Alibaba and ByteDance can argue the profit comes from their models and customers, so paying the tax at headquarters is reasonable. That is a fair point, yet it leaves the host area in the lurch. Ulanqab can keep the tax paid during construction and the taxes on land and buildings, but neither will grow the way sales do to support sustainable development.
As the national “East Data, West Computing” program moves data centers west to power China’s AI push, other western places that host data centers face the same arithmetic – unless the invoicing companies register there. Ulanqab’s 109 signed data-center projects are expected to come online within two to three years. Once construction stops, the city’s tax take from computing may stop growing, and with it the chance to turn data centers into lasting development.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic Revenue Hits Nearly $17 Billion Before Blockbuster IPO
articles.title_zh: Anthropic Revenue Hits Nearly $17 Billion Before Blockbuster IPO
articles.content_orig:
Author of the AI Insider newsletter
Here's a remarkable milestone in the AI revolution: Anthropic now spends more on internal AI usage than it does paying employees.
The company revealed this in its IPO filing . In April, the value of Claude AI used internally, calculated at prices Anthropic charges customers, exceeded its monthly employee compensation costs, excluding stock awards.
By September, that internal AI usage had surged more than 250-fold since January.
There's an important distinction here. Anthropic isn't actually spending more cash on AI than salaries. It's valuing its internal AI consumption at retail prices.
Still, this feels like a watershed moment for the tech industry.
In March, I wrote about a new trend : Tech companies are starting to treat AI tokens (the main way to measure usage) as a fourth component of employee compensation, alongside salary, bonuses, and stock awards.
Anthropic's numbers show why. More than 90% of the code added to its software in September was written by Claude. Meanwhile, revenue has grown vastly faster than headcount.
For decades, talented humans were the most valuable resource in Silicon Valley. Now AI is challenging that assumption.

Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Monday. Read our full coverage here.
Iran's 2-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, resume nuclear talks
Iran said it had a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the U.S. if Washington meets its demands.
The announcement came as the region braces for possible renewed fighting, even as Iran’s top diplomat said Sunday that he hoped the U.S. would choose “diplomacy over other paths.”
Iran previously said the plan could be implemented within a week if the U.S. met seven conditions, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports. Iran now says ships passing through the reopened strait would have to follow a route agreed upon by Iran and Oman and travel under Iranian supervision. Separately, Iranian officials have said the U.S. must lift sanctions on Iranian oil sales and agree to a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said the plan remained the basis for negotiations with Washington through mediators, despite the shorter implementation timeline. “This once again demonstrates Iran’s good-faith approach,” he added.
Baghaei gave no indication that Tehran had changed its demands or that Washington had accepted its proposal.
President Donald Trump has alternated between pursuing diplomacy and threatening heavy bombing of Iran in his public comments.
More than 300,000 Yemenis have fled fighting, UN says
The U.N. migration agency said the people are struggling to find shelter and life essentials, as aid groups face limited access to those in need.
They have fled as renewed fighting between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government forces broke a four-year truce, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian situation in one of the Middle East's poorest countries.
Taiz province, in southwestern Yemen, continues to take in displaced families, but many are fleeing south to Aden, which has now received more than 56,000 people, according to the latest figures by the International Organization for Migration.
“After years of conflict, families in Yemen are being forced to flee yet again, often with little more than the clothes on their backs,” Abdusattor Esoev, head of the IOM's mission in Yemen, said Sunday.
“They urgently need shelter, food, clean water and health care. Without more funding, thousands of families could be left without the help they urgently need,” he added.
China to send special envoy to Iran and the Gulf
China said Monday it plans to send a special envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters the envoy would focus on easing tensions and promoting regional stability.
The Gulf region “should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict,” Chinese President Xi Jinping told Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said on Monday, according to a readout of their meeting.
The move comes as China seeks to expand its influence in the rapidly changing region, which it depends on for a large share of its oil.
Two Israeli airstrikes killed two men in southern Gaza early Monday, according to Nasser Hospital, where their bodies were taken. One strike killed a man in his home; the other killed a man in a tent.
The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Major fighting between Israel and Hamas largely halted under the October 2025 ceasefire. Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes on Gaza that it says target militants, though the strikes regularly kill or injure women and children. Israel says Hamas uses civilians as human shields.
About 1,580 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began, bringing the overall death toll to more than 74,500, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, does not distinguish between civilians and militants.

articles.content_orig:
After many months of discussion , Apple has figured out a way to bring Apple Intelligence to China, working with Alibaba’s Qwen model on some features. Apple Intelligence will soon be made available as a developer beta and will ship to Chinese customers in December with iOS 27.3.
China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology approved the use of Alibaba AI models with the iPhone in October 2026. Confirming the complexity of bringing these tools to China, Apple also received clearance in July from the Cyberspace Administration of China. Apple watchers are at liberty to reflect that the news comes at the best possible time for the company, which continues to grow smartphone market share in China.
The promise of integrated AI support in the form of Apple Intelligence can only boost interest in the company’s recently introduced iPhone Duo . Recent Counterpoint Research data claims iPhone sales increased 29% year on year in China in the three weeks following launch of the 18 Pro series devices. Initial stock of the devices sold out in hours.
China is also the world’s biggest market for foldable devices, which prompted some enterprising individuals to attempt to resell purchased iPhone Duos for far above their store price — scalpers have since reduced prices , because even in iPhone-crazy China, people weren’t willing to pay so much.
While it’s a big step for Apple AI in China, it’s not quite the great leap Apple may have wanted to put in place.
Siri AI is not supported and won’t be “anytime soon,” according to market speculation . While little is said about the reasons for that, it seems probable that political pressure in both the US and China may be partly to blame, as both nations see control of the means of AI production as essential for the future success of their differing ideologies. Apple has had to allow the Chinese government to approve ongoing updates to the suite.
Chinese users can use Alibaba’s Qwen in Siri, writing tools, and visual intelligence, including functions related to text and image understanding. They don’t get Image Playground, but can expect:
Apple and Alibaba also promise to maintain privacy. Customers will be able to choose if they wish to proceed with making a request through Qwen. Alibaba also said it would not use these requests for model training, though it isn’t yet clear if requests are going to Private Cloud Compute in Apple’s Chinese AI deployment.
Will the introduction of Apple Intelligence in China make a difference? It probably already is, as months of ever stronger speculation mean most Chinese consumers knew Apple AI was coming to their iPhones even as they purchased them before the announcement took place.
While the initial sales rush on Apple’s new devices among Chinese consumers has slowed, the news may help generate fresh enthusiasm for the iPhone in China. That’s great for Apple, but not such great news for some smaller smartphone vendors, who continue to be hammered by vicious increases in memory and other component prices.
Speaking almost two years ago when industry observers had anticipated an Apple Intelligence launch in China would take place earlier, Morgan Stanley then suggested the Alibaba partnership would be “a critical catalyst for Apple’s competitive standing in China.”
Other than painful price increases, not much has changed, and the introduction can only help consolidate the iPhone’s appeal in China. That’s good for Apple’s customers there, and great news for Apple’s investors everywhere else. It may even do something to retain a little US soft power.
In the background, we see the continued economic pressure wrought by fast-increasing memory prices. This has driven smartphone makers to raise prices, which has itself driven a 21% year on year decline in sector sales .
Apple and Samsung have proved more resilient to these price hikes than others, which means the added appeal generated by the launch of Apple Intelligence in the world’s second-largest economy is likely to make a highly significant difference to its market share in the short term, as well as shoring up share in future replacement cycles.

These days I write my daily AppleHolic blog at Computerworld.com, where I explore Apple's growing identity in the enterprise. You can also keep up with my work at AppleMust , and follow me on BlueSky , Mastodon , and LinkedIn .

articles.title_zh: New Samsung Galaxy S27+ certification confirms its charging prowess - GSMArena.com news
articles.content_orig:
The upcoming Samsung Galaxy S27+ showed up in China's 3C database with 45W charging support back in September, and now another certification is backing that up. A couple of safety certifications list the phone with a 15V/3A rating, which works out to 45W.
Between them, the two certifications cover pretty much every version of the handset, from the global SM-S956B and the Korean SM-S956N to the US SM-S956U, the Chinese SM-S9560, and the SC-52H headed to Docomo in Japan. In other words, it looks like the S27+ will charge at the same speed wherever you buy it.
Samsung Galaxy S27+ new certification
That's the same 45W you get with the Galaxy S26+ , which means Samsung's Plus models are set to stay at that speed for a sixth generation in a row, ever since the Galaxy S22+ . The vanilla Galaxy S27 isn't getting a bump either, since its own certification last week pointed to the same 25W as the Galaxy S26 . The Galaxy S27 series is rumored to return to the usual January/February launch window , so we shouldn't have to wait too long for all of this to be officially confirmed.

articles.title_orig: China steps up Middle East diplomacy with Iran and Oman meetings
articles.title_zh: China steps up Middle East diplomacy with Iran and Oman meetings
articles.content_orig:
China is stepping up its diplomatic efforts in the Middle East, including over the US-Israel war on Iran , following a lapse in activity.
Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Monday met a senior Iranian security official in Beijing, while President Xi Jinping hosted Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq for a landmark state visit.
Wang told Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, that dialogue and negotiation remained “the only viable path forward” as conflicts in the region “drag on and risk further spillover”.
He also reaffirmed China’s support for Iran’s sovereignty and security. Beijing has consistently blamed the US and Israel for starting the conflict.
“China is very close to Tehran; it is the biggest trading partner of Iran, the biggest customer of Iranian crude,” said Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu, reporting from Beijing.
However, Beijing’s diplomacy efforts have recently been stalled, she noted.
“It’s been a few weeks or even months [in which] China really hasn’t done much diplomatically towards … ending the war,” Yu said.
The meetings on Monday appear to illustrate that China is growing impatient with the lack of progress.
“I think China is very frustrated, and it wants to be seen to enter [the process],” Yu said.
Reflecting the step up in activity, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced on Monday that Zhai Jun, Beijing’s special envoy on the Middle East, will visit Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia this month.
Meanwhile, Xi received Sultan Haitham, the first Omani head of state to visit China since the two countries established diplomatic relations in 1978.
The Chinese president said the Middle East and Gulf “should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict”.
Sitting across from Iran on the Strait of Hormuz, Oman is a key player in navigation on the strategic waterway, through which one-fifth of global energy exports traversed before the US-Iran war restricted traffic.
China is one of the world’s largest energy importers. Xi described bilateral ties with Oman as being at a “new historical starting point”.
During the visit, China and Oman signed 14 cooperation documents, covering areas including artificial intelligence, green energy and supply chains, along with a currency swap agreement.
In a joint statement, they called for safe navigation to resume through Hormuz and urged the US and Iran to restart dialogue.
Yu said the conflict had made the relationship “more of a priority for both sides”, particularly given the disruption to China’s energy imports.
“Oman is particularly important because many of its ports are outside the strait,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Cyberattacks hit supermarket fridges and freezers in Europe, Belgium launches investigation
articles.title_zh: Cyberattacks hit supermarket fridges and freezers in Europe, Belgium launches investigation
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of supermarkets in Europe have reported temperatures of their refrigerators and fridges rising overnight, now widely believed to be caused by cyber attacks similar to the one that affected France several weeks ago.
Supermarket chains in Belgium, Sweden, Estonia, Netherlands, Luxembourg and Ireland have been affected.
The story began with Belgian media reporting on Monday that fridges were turned up to 17 degrees Celsius, forcing many stores to throw away food.
Belgium's Centre for Cybersecurity (CCB) told Belgian outlet Belga that it is aware of an incident targeting supermarket refrigeration systems.
CCB spokesperson Katrien Eggers told Euronews Next, "We are aware of an incident, but have no further information." There are no reports yet as to who was behind the attack... and it may never be possible to identify them."
Belgium's federal prosecutor's office have opened an investigation into the incident, according to a spokesperson.
Some 40 Delhaize Proxy supermarkets, 15 Carrefour Shop & Go stores, 15 Intermarché shops and five Spar Q8 service station locations have reportedly been impacted in Belgium, according to Belgian outlet Le Soir .
Butchery group De Laet en Van Haver also said that their fridges were affected. IKEA have also said their Bergen shop located at Mons was affected, bringing the total to 75 stores affected in Belgium.
"We have identified an IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in several dozen stores. We immediately took the necessary measures to keep our stores operational," a spokesperson from Delhaize told Euronews Next.
Carrefour told Euronews Next this morning that "the impact at Carrefour is very limited: currently 15 of our 700 stores are affected, both in Flanders and Wallonia. Not a single hypermarket is among them."
"All stores remain open because it only concerns a few refrigeration units, mainly freezers. Quick action was taken so that all stores can stay open," they added.
Meanwhile later this morning Carrefour Belgium spokesman Mich Vergauwen said, "It's a cyberattack, there is no other reason," adding that the "impact is very limited".
It's believed the incident took place between Sunday night and Monday morning, skyrocketing refrigerator temperatures.
Stephan Moelans, CEO of refrigeration installer Sabcobel, which manages Delhaize's fridges and freeze systems, told the Belga news outlet that the Belgian attack involves exactly the same mechanism as the previous French cyberattack.
"Over the past few weeks, we've been working very hard to protect our customers' fridges against this vulnerability," Moelans said.
He said the incident happened when the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode.
The refrigeration executive said a software update alone is not enough to address the vulnerability, with physical modifications required instead.
"That requires investment. The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France."
Sabcobel know of around twenty affected units, out of the hundreds it manages across Belgium.
Danfoss, the company that supplied the software for the refrigeration systems affected in both the latest incident and the one in France in October, said customers who had not updated their software were affected.
A spokesperson told VTM NIEUWS that "the company says that the vulnerability lies primarily in outdated software and that they had already urged customers to start using their new software".
Problems reportedly also occurred at a number of stores of the Swedish supermarket chains ICA and Coop last night, with refrigerators and freezers turned up to 50 degrees Celsius.
A similar incident occurred in Estonian at one location of supermarket chain Selver, according to media reports.
13 SuperValu stores in Ireland were affected by a suspected cyber incident, according to a statement by owner Musgrave made to the Irish Times.
In the Netherlands, the freezing and cooling systems of at least seventeen companies were attacked last night, according to a spokesperson for supplier Danfoss. The identities of the companies were not disclosed.
Delhaize also suspended its ordering systems in Luxembourg as a precaution to prevent a similar incident.
Finnish media report that several K Group supermarkets have been affected. K Group is one of Finland's largest retail chains.
These reported incidents follow a similar attack in France just weeks ago, on 12 October, when hundreds of French supermarkets belonging to the Intermarché and Coopérative U chains fell victim to a cyberattack targeting their refrigeration systems.

articles.title_orig: Stealth Classic Thief: The Dark Project Returns for a PS5 Remaster with New Content
articles.title_zh: Stealth Classic Thief: The Dark Project Returns for a PS5 Remaster with New Content
articles.content_orig:
One of the classics that helped create an entire genre, stealth masterpiece Thief: The Dark Project is coming to PS5 in remastered form next month, from 3rd December 2026.
This new version of the 1998 game has been remastered using Nightdive Studios' KEX Engine to produce a new edition running at 4K and 120 frames-per-second. It's got all the content of the base game, the three extra missions from Thief: Gold, and an entirely new campaign in the form of The Tarnished Mirror.
The Tarnished Mirror is a narrative bridge between The Dark Project and Thief 2: The Metal Age . In it, "a seemingly straightforward theft spirals into imprisonment, uneasy alliances and a descent into a drowned, R’lyeh-like necropolis. Players will experience an expanded enemy roster, ambitious level design and a pure Thief experience that descends into unsettling, otherworldly horror."
Subscribe to Push Square on YouTube 172k
The bonus campaign has been created by the same people who made Thief: The Black Parade , which was a mod / expansion for Thief: Gold, made by the fans. "This collaboration marks a rare industry moment, with Nightdive and Eidos-Montréal welcoming a community creation directly into official canon," the press release added.
You can also expect the following from the remastered package:
Pre-orders are live on the PS Store for the PS5 digital versions, with a standard edition costing £24.99 / $29.99 and a Digital Deluxe Edition priced at £28.99 / $34.99.
In terms of physical editions, you're looking at three versions to choose from: standard, steelbook, and deluxe trapezoid. The first two are self-explanatory, but the Deluxe Trapezoid edition includes the game, steelbook, booklet, a box, and a physical remaster diary for £49.99 / $69.99:

articles.title_orig: Spain train crash: US, Japan and Canada citizens among dead, authorities say
articles.title_zh: Spain train crash: US, Japan and Canada citizens among dead, authorities say
articles.content_orig:
Dr Marta Shahbazi, pictured in 2024, was travelling to collect a prize at an awards ceremony in her native Spain when she died
An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.
Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to an awards ceremony on Wednesday when the train she was on crashed into another near Urda, south of Madrid, killing 69 people.
The mother of two was an affiliate associate professor leading a group of researchers at MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) in Cambridge and had earned several awards for work on human embryos and cell biology.
In a statement, the LMB paid tribute to the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist" and described her death as a "profound shock and a huge loss".
The expert in cell biology ran the Shahbazi Laboratory at the LMB, based on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus.
She had been announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development and  was due to collect the award at a conference in El Rompido in Andalusia.
The LMB said: "As a wife and mother of two young children, Marta wrote eloquently about balancing her family and career, serving as a much-admired role model for a 'mother scientist', a term she used to describe herself.
"Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies," the LMB said.
The institute said her death was "a profound shock and a huge loss for LMB".
Her work had been recognised with "many awards and prizes", the laboratory added.
Shahbazi joined the Cambridge laboratory in 2020
Shahbazi is listed on the University of Cambridge website as a principal investigator at its Stem Cell Institute (CSCI).
Institute director Prof Bertie Gottgens said its community was "shocked and deeply saddened" by her death.
"Marta led her primary research group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) alongside her roles as an affiliate principal investigator and affiliate assistant professor at the CSCI," he said.
"Across both institutes, she was highly respected for her pioneering research on early human development and valued for her collaborative spirit.
"Her creativity, passion, and generosity will be greatly missed."
The news of her death was first confirmed in a social media post , external by the CiMUS, based in Santiago de Compostela where Shahbazi's aunt works.
Shahbazi undertook her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre, before joining the University of Cambridge as a post-doctoral fellow and then the LMB in 2020.
The crash in Spain happened when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company.
It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Three days of national mourning were declared in the country.
More than 540 people were on board both trains.

articles.title_orig: Stock market after midterm elections: What S&P 500 history shows
articles.title_zh: Stock market after midterm elections: What S&P 500 history shows
articles.content_orig:
Markets are sweating it out ahead of the midterm elections, but the event historically heralds strong performance for stocks — regardless of whether it's a red or blue wave, split decision, or status quo in Washington.
The S&P 500 tends to perform well after both midterm and presidential elections. According to a CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns after elections from 1980 through 2024, the index rose an average of 0.2% after one day and one week, and 1.1% after one month across both presidential and midterm elections.
A year later, the index gained an average of 13.7% after midterms and 13.8% after presidential elections. Returns were positive in 91% of cases. And the S&P 500 was up after all 11 midterms from 1982 through 2022.
Short-term returns were less reliable, particularly after presidential contests, which produced slightly negative average returns after one day and one week.
"There's some anxiousness before these elections," Ryan Detrick, CNBC contributor and chief market strategist at Carson Group, told CNBC. "Once you are through it, it's a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well."
Still, the market usually prefers divided government: one party in charge of the White House and the other holding at least one house of Congress.
Across 10 midterm and five presidential elections that left no single party in charge, the S&P 500 rose an average 15% after one year. One-year returns were positive in 14 out of 15 cases. By comparison, the index gained an average of 11.5% over the year after elections that resulted in single-party control.
"If you have a huge red wave or a big blue wave, markets actually kind of don't like that as much because you have too much spending one way and too much power," Detrick said.
Leaving Democrats in control of Congress with a Republican in the White House — a scenario that may emerge from the elections on Tuesday — was also positive. A CNBC analysis found that after the three midterms (1986, 1990 and 2006) when Democrats controlled both houses and a Republican held the presidency, the S&P 500 averaged a 0.5% decline on the reaction day but was up 3.4% a month later and 10.9% after a year.
Granted, elections may be coincident events to factors that matter far more for market performance.
The S&P 500 plunged 22.1% in the year after the 2000 elections due to the dotcom bust, marking the worst post-election performance since 1980. Conversely, the S&P 500's best post-election year was a 38.3% gain after the 2020 elections, when markets mounted a massive comeback from the COVID-induced selloff.
Investors should bear in mind that Federal Reserve policy and the corporate earnings cycle ultimately matter more than elections, according to Société Générale.
Stocks declined in the aftermath of the 2018 midterms, for instance, when Democrats wrested control of the House during President Donald Trump's first term. More importantly, the Fed tightened monetary policy that year, raising interest rates four times, and the S&P 500 ended the year down 6.2%, though the market was up 11.7% a year after the election.
The big swing factor now is AI and whether declines in tech will continue. As long as the AI wave is still moving and the economy keeps growing, "this bull market is probably still alive and well," Detrick says.
But a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate would almost certainly pressure the AI infrastructure buildout and could lead to more retrenchment.
The bond market is also skittish with yields rising globally and a mini debt crisis in France. And the war with Iran could get worse post-election if President Trump follows through on threats of more strikes or Iran escalates.
"Seasonality isn't destiny, and worries around Iran, AI and France won't mysteriously vanish," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note.
If history is any guide, we could see a Santa rally and S&P 500 gains after the midterms. But this is still an AI-driven market, with geopolitics, the Fed, and bond market very much in charge.
— CNBC's Chris Hayes contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Honda Africa Twin range gets bigger engine, fresh technology, and brand-new model lines
articles.title_zh: Honda Africa Twin range gets bigger engine, fresh technology, and brand-new model lines
articles.content_orig:
Honda have announced major changes to their Africa Twin adventure bike family for 2027, confirming new models, plus a capacity jump from 1084cc to 1131cc across the line-up.
Now known as the CRF1150L, the range will consist of a standard base model, plus the road-focussed Adventure Sports (AS) as before. A new off-road centric Enduro Sports will also join the brigade, with a raised front mudguard and spoked 21in front wheel.
Starting with the Adventure Sports, the base version will be joined by a new top of the line CRF1150L Africa Twin Adventure Sports Honda Sensing Ride – fitted with front and rear radar to compete against the likes of the new Triumph Tiger 1200 , and fully-specced BMW R1300GS .
Exclusively available with Honda’s semi-automatic Dual Clutch Transmission (DCT) system, the Sensing Ride is joined by two standard CRF1150L AS variants – one with a conventional manual gearbox and another with DCT in place.
All three are expected in UK dealers from March and put out a claimed 117.3bhp at 7500rpm and 87.8lb.ft of torque at 5750rpm, with the updated parallel-twin motor housed in a revised steel frame which – combined with an aluminium swingarm – cuts a claimed 1.4kg over the outgoing structure.
That’s not to say the bikes are lightweights though – far from it – with kerb weights starting at 245kg for the conventional manual, raising to 255kg for the AS with DCT. The Sensing Ride version tips the scales at 256kg – with all three getting 220mm of ground clearance and an adjustable seat height of between 830-850mm.
All three are fed by a 24.2-litre fuel tank, with Honda promising 55.4mpg for the manual version and 52.3mpg for the semi-automatic flavours. This fuel tank runs under the seat, which Honda says helps contribute to a greater mass centralisation of weight – helping the bikes to feel less top heavy and potentially more composed on the go.
This is combined with a re-positioned battery, ECU, fuel filler cap, and airbox – with Honda also keen to make life easier when manoeuvring at low speeds, especially handy when loaded up with luggage and/or a pillion passenger .
Being the road-biased version, all three roll on a 19in front and 18in rear spoked wheel, shod with a choice of Bridgestone Battlax Adventure A41s, or Michelin Anakee Roads.
Not only this, but the riding position has also been tweaked, with the handlebars now 10mm narrower and 10mm higher and further forward. The footpegs are also 10mm further forward and 20mm narrower, too.
Away from the numbers, the Africa Twins are now even cleverer than before, with Honda promising six standard riding modes that can all be personalised to the rider’s preferences. There’s also an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) for lean-sensitive rider modes, and backlit switchgear that’s said to be less complex than the current design.
The Sensing Ride takes this further with front and rear radar guidance – a first for the Africa Twin – unlocking rider support including blind spot detection, adaptive cruise control, and group ride assistance.
Alongside this, you’ll also find front and rearward collision warnings, plus ‘Distance Assist’ (to stop you getting too close to the vehicle in front on a manual throttle), and an ‘Emergency Brake Assist’ that applies some stopping power when there is a collision risk up front.
Being the clutchless DCT variant, it also gets ‘Stop & Go’, which lets the bike follow the vehicle in front during stop start traffic – a similar set-up to the semi-automatic KTM 1390 Super Adventure S Evo , launched for the beginning of 2026.
It doesn’t end there either because the Adventure Sports trio come on Showa electronic suspension as standard, known as Electronically Equipped Ride Adjustment (or EERA for short).
Working through a monoshock and chunky 49mm upside down front forks (up from 45mm), it is combined with Honda Skyhook control that continuously monitors the position of the bike to adjust damping forces in a bid improve handling, stability, and ride quality.
The EERA system itself takes data from sources including the ECU, IMU and fork stroke sensor to adjust damping by the millisecond – with 210mm of travel available at the front end, and 200mm available at the rear.
As is the way with many modern adventure bikes, a ‘Minimum’ mode will also lower the seat height by 5mm for a flatter foot and remains selected even after you’ve switched off the bike.
There’s also a raft of preload settings too, consisting of ‘Solo’, ‘Solo with Luggage’, ‘Pillion’, and ‘Pillion with Full Luggage’. Adjustment can then be further fine-tuned, including 24-steps of preload – with further electronic interventions including hill hold control, and electronically combined ABS that monitors brake pressure in the calipers at both ends for smoother applications.
Alongside the Adventure Sports comes a new CRF1150L Africa Twin Enduro Sports model, which shares many of the same creature comforts, but comes based around the updated standard model.
Promising a 9kg weight reduction, it’s distinguish it from its siblings by a pointed front beak, and HRC-style paint – however performance still comes from the same new 1131cc parallel-twin engine, meaning an identical 117.3bhp at 7500rpm and 87.8lb.ft of torque at 5750rpm.
Just like the standard model, it rolls on a 21in front and 18in spoked rim with tubeless Metzeler Karoo Street tyres, and shares the same steel frame, aluminium swingarm, riding position, electronics, and updated seven inch TFT display (with additional 5.7in screen) – with a choice of manual or DCT gearboxes available to order.
Keyless ignition, cruise control, and handguards come as standard – as do six customisable riding modes, plus an adjustable seat height of between 870mm and 890mm plus a kerb weight of 228kg for the manual and 239kg for the DCT.
Like the Adventure Sports, you’ll find CarPlay and Android Auto, with the bike receiving a higher 260mm of ground clearance and fully-adjustable 49mm closed-cartridge forks inspired by the brand’s CRF450 Rally competition bike.
Suspension comes via Showa at both ends, with 240mm of travel up front and 230mm at the rear. This works with sizeable 310mm floating wavey front discs, plus an advanced array of lean-sensitive electronics including seven stage Honda Selectable Torque Control (or traction control) which meters the amount of intervention on the throttle on- or off-road, depending on inputs from the six-axis IMU.
Other features include wheelie control, and traction can be switched off altogether if required. Unlike the Adventure Sports, the fuel capacity drops to 18.8 litres, thanks to an altered dual-tank design – however the same overall adventure bike silhouette remains.
Although still sitting at the lower end of the big adventure bike power figures, Honda’s Africa Twin motor has undergone some significant development for 2027.
For starters, there’s a redesigned intake system, plus larger-diameter 52mm throttle bodies (up from 46mm), and a revised valvetrain and cylinder head – with Honda promising an increased compression ratio from 10.5:1 to now 12.1:1.
The pistons have also changed, as have the con rods, crankshaft and balancer shafts – with options for both a six-speed manual or semi-automatic Dual Clutch Transmission system (that both share the same crankcase design).
Honda have brought the Africa Twin right up-to-date with these changes, however the fresh engine is still lacking the performance figures of some its premium big-capacity rivals. Whether you need all that punch is debatable, but the fresh electronics and revised riding position should make it a strong contender whether you fancy a trip across Europe by road, or by trail.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street's Fear Index is doing something strange. Here's what it means for stocks
articles.title_zh: Wall Street's Fear Index is doing something strange. Here's what it means for stocks
articles.content_orig:
Stocks wrapped their worst week since June on Friday, but a group of the most sophisticated options analysts agree the reaction in the options market was oddly calm.
While the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) , often referred to as a so-called fear index, did touch its highest intraday level since April on Friday, it quickly retreated and closed at 19.4. Its rollover came even as the S&P 500 finished the day down nearly 2%. For that size of a decline in stocks, the 2.2-point move in VIX was "relatively muted," according to SpotGamma's Brent Kochuba, whose analysis suggests VIX should have jumped closer to 2.6 points, based on a study of 126 selloffs since 2018.
Even in the Nasdaq 100 Index , where implied volatility increased for most options contracts, there were key exceptions. Prices on put contracts that are between 20% and 50% out-of-the-money were higher on a volatility basis after the sell-off on Oct. 16, according to data shared by Nasdaq's Kevin Davitt.
So not only did traders not pile into S&P 500 Index options on Friday, they were also especially choosy with which Nasdaq hedges they bought. For example, in the Nasdaq, puts were more expensive two weeks ago, according to Nations Indexes data. And out-of-the-money S&P 500 Index puts "just aren't being chased-into at this moment," writes Nomura managing director Charlie McElligott, indicating investor calm in the face of falling stocks.
"Index options skew hasn't been particularly reactive to the few days of spot equities selloff this week, and even where it has, it's partially a function of call vol getting mushed," McElligot said in a note to clients on Friday.
One explanation for the lack of hedging could be that asset managers are quickly selling stocks instead of using options to protect those stocks from further decline.
One popular chart making the rounds over the weekend came from Morgan Stanley's prime brokerage. According to the firm's data on long-short active managers, total global gross equity exposure is down 8% from its most recent peak, the biggest drawdown in at least ten years.
"Long/short has experienced a massive de-levering event," said Zed Francis, CIO of Chicago-based Convexitas. "Buy the shorts, sell the longs. If you were closer to cash than you were before, no need to hedge. I believe this is the main reason implied volatility has remained quiet during an increased-stress month."

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu and Eisenkot Seek Shot to Be Israel’s Premier
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu and Eisenkot Seek Shot to Be Israel’s Premier
articles.content_orig:
President Isaac Herzog will begin consultations with representatives of the parties elected to the 26th Knesset on Wednesday, starting with the smallest factions in an unusual departure from previous rounds of coalition negotiations, the President's Office announced on Monday.
Rather than beginning with the largest parties, Herzog will invite faction representatives in ascending order of Knesset seats, beginning with Religious Zionism-Zehut and concluding with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud on Thursday evening.
According to the President's Office, the decision is intended to "encourage thinking outside the box," allowing Herzog to consider a wider range of potential coalition arrangements before consulting with the larger factions.
The consultations come as Israel's political parties face the challenge of forming a governing coalition following the October 27 election, with neither of the two largest parties, Likud and Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, enjoying a straightforward path to a 61-seat majority.
Herzog has emphasized the importance of exploring potential compromises to prevent another election, with the unusual consultation order potentially allowing smaller factions to present alternative coalition arrangements before the president meets with Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
In his statement, Herzog said he would hear the positions of all factions, seeking to "exhaust every possibility, broaden the dialogue, and explore any avenue that could advance the process."
The president also left open the possibility of holding a second round of consultations if necessary.
The consultations will begin Wednesday at 5 p.m. with Religious Zionism-Zehut, followed by Shas at 6:15 p.m. and Yisrael Beytenu at 7:30 p.m.
Meetings will resume Thursday morning, beginning with United Torah Judaism at 8:30 a.m., followed by Otzma Yehudit at 9:45 a.m., the Democrats at 11 a.m., and Ra'am at 12:15 p.m.
Following an afternoon break, Herzog will meet with the Joint List at 4:45 p.m., B'Yachad at 6 p.m., Yashar at 7:15 p.m., and finally Likud at 8:30 p.m.
During the consultations, each faction will be given an opportunity to recommend a Knesset member to receive the mandate to form the next government.
While the number of recommendations each candidate receives matters, the president is not legally required to select the candidate with the most recommendations. Instead, Herzog must determine which Knesset member has the best chance of successfully forming a government.
Under Basic Law: The Government, the Knesset member entrusted with forming a government has 28 days to assemble a coalition. The president may grant an extension of up to 14 additional days if necessary.
Should the designated candidate fail to form a government, the law provides for further procedures that could see another Knesset member given the opportunity to assemble a coalition.
The consultations will be broadcast live on the president's official social media accounts, allowing the public to follow the parties' recommendations and the opening stages of the coalition-building process.

articles.title_orig: Suspected cyberattacks trigger supermarket fridge failures across Europe
articles.title_zh: Suspected cyberattacks trigger supermarket fridge failures across Europe
articles.content_orig:
Suspected cyberattacks have triggered temperatures to rise in grocery store refrigeration systems in a growing number of countries across Europe.
Overnight temperature spikes were recorded in stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden. On Monday, retailers and authorities pointed to alleged cyberattacks that underscored the vulnerability of systems that once largely operated mechanically.
The head of ⁠⁠⁠⁠Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, confirmed on Monday to the Reuters news agency that the centre ⁠⁠⁠⁠is responding to ⁠⁠⁠⁠multiple incidents affecting store cooling systems.
“We have in recent weeks … identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch,” he said.
The temperature of freezers in several Swedish stores rose suddenly overnight, store operators ICA and Coop said, while Swedish retailer Axfood said freezers at a distribution centre for home delivery of groceries in the Gothenburg area were hacked.
SuperValu, Ireland’s third-largest supermarket chain, ⁠⁠⁠⁠said a specific model of refrigeration systems has been affected by a “cyber incident” at 13 of its 223 ⁠⁠⁠⁠stores.
The Belga news agency reported overnight temperature increases at dozens of ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Ahold Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg. They were blamed on a cyberattack, according to the chief ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠executive ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠of refrigeration company,⁠ ⁠⁠⁠Sabcobel.
Stephan Moelans said the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.
Also in Belgium, five Spar shops had their fridge systems attacked, said a spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates the franchise system.
In Estonia, at least one supermarket chain was affected, technology supplier Kitman Coldtech told public broadcaster ERR.
“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” Kitman’s CEO Jann Mutso said, without naming the affected chain.
Ahold Delhaize reported a cybersecurity incident to Dutch police last month.
The cyberattack on refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets in France raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F), spoiling food and causing fires at several stores.
One Swedish store said in a social media post on Monday that the temperature of its refrigerators and freezers had been set to the same temperature as during the cyberattack in France.
“We are aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems,” a spokesperson for privately held ICA told Reuters in an email.
Kitman’s Mutso also said that temperatures at the Estonian chain were set to 50 degrees Celsius (122F).
Privately-held retailer Coop told Swedish daily Aftonbladet that six of its stores had been affected by similar incidents.
There has been no claim of responsibility for Monday’s attack, nor the one earlier in France.
However, the incidents help to increase concern regarding hybrid warfare stemming from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Iran-United States war.
European states have blamed Moscow for a growing number of incidents affecting infrastructure, including via cyberattacks, in recent months. Russia has repeatedly denied involvement in any sabotage or hybrid warfare operations.
European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen said the attacks were “a deliberate attempt ⁠to disrupt” EU food supplies and undermine public ‌confidence.
“These incidents show that cyberattacks ⁠can disrupt services, affect ⁠businesses and directly affect citizens’ ⁠daily lives”, a ⁠European Commission spokesperson ⁠said, stressing the importance of strengthening ‌cybersecurity across the bloc.
A spokesperson for The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium told Al Jazeera that the rising number of cyberattack incidents, especially those resulting from the targeted use of AI, is an evolving trend.
However, they added, “we may never be able to identify … who is behind this attack”.

articles.title_orig: iPadOS 27.2 adds convenient new multitasking option on iPad
articles.title_zh: iPadOS 27.2 adds convenient new multitasking option on iPad
articles.content_orig:
iPadOS 27.2 launched last week with a variety of new features for iPad, including a convenient change for multitasking.
When iPhone Duo first got into users’ hands, several reviews mentioned how the new Split View system felt more intuitive than iPadOS multitasking ever has.
And in iPadOS 27.2, there’s a convenient new multitasking change that’s likely inspired by iPhone Duo.
Apple hasn’t brought over the entire iOS system to the iPad. But it has made one common multitasking feature easier to set up: Split View.
From the official iPadOS 27.2 release notes:
Side-by-side multitasking is easier to set up with the option to choose a second app whenever you tile apps to the left or right with the window controls or menu bar
Starting with iPadOS 26 last year, setting up two apps side-by-side could fairly cumbersome.
You needed to open the first app, resize it, then swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see your other apps, select one, and in many cases manually resize the second app too.
But in iPadOS 27.2, any time you use Apple’s window resizing controls to tile an app left or right, you’ll immediately see the Home Screen and be able to tile a second app with a single tap.
It’s not identical to the iPhone Duo experience, but it’s a lot closer to it than the old system was.
Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side.
What do you think of this multitasking change in iPadOS 27.2? Do you think Apple should apply its iPhone Duo learnings to the iPad? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Arab parties back Eisenkot: What’s the latest in Israel’s coalition talks?
articles.title_zh: Arab parties back Eisenkot: What’s the latest in Israel’s coalition talks?
articles.content_orig:
Yousef Jabareen says he is ready to join forces with opposition bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu after winning record number of seats in Knesset
The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition, which holds the balance of power after Tuesday’s elections, has said the country is facing a historic opportunity to change direction.
Yousef Jabareen, the head of the Joint List, said he was ready to join forces with the “Change” bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition, and to wrest control of the Knesset.
Turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, 20% of the population) more than doubled to about 80% , transforming the political landscape. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote.
Jabareen said the first demand of the roughly 840,000 Palestinian Israeli voters was to get rid of the Netanyahu government, and in particular its most extreme members , Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister.
“This has been an awful four years … in all areas of life: in terms of house demolition, criminal gangs within the Arab community without any [intervention] from the police; not allocating the needed resources for our municipalities, for our education, for our youth in general; racism in all areas of life – physical attacks against Arabs, the brutality of the police,” Jabareen told the Guardian in one of his first interviews since the election. “So this has been really a very dangerous period.”
He said the next few days would be critical. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, is due to summon political leaders as early as Wednesday to canvass their recommendations on who should be given the first chance to form the next government, with no single grouping commanding a clear claim on power.
Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by the retired general Gadi Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving the Arab-Israeli parties as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.
Eisenkot and his partners have pledged not to form a unity government with Netanyahu, but Eisenkot has also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties: they have to recognise that Israel is a Jewish state, accept compulsory national service – either civil or military – and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, have signalled it is ready to join an Eisenkot coalition. The Joint List has no intention of joining such a government, but Jabareen said the coalition was ready to keep it afloat from the outside with tactical voting in the Knesset.
“The conditions that [Eisenkot] speaks of are more relevant for parties who would be in the coalition. We are not planning to be in the coalition … for very clear reasons,” Jabareen said at his family home in the northern city of Umm al-Fahm. “As long as the occupation of our people in the West Bank continues, we cannot be part of a government.
“However, in order to use our political power to get rid of the extreme Netanyahu government, we said that we will consider the possibility of supporting from outside. This is an opportunity to change policies, to change attitudes, including towards the Arab community and towards the Palestinian people.
“This is really a historic moment and I hope that there will be partners within the opposition to go ahead with that. We are thinking that this could be the start of a change.”
Jabareen, 54, a former law professor and the leader of the socialist Hadash party, has yet to talk to Eisenkot since Tuesday’s elections, but he confirmed that informal discussions among opposition parties were under way.
Forming a new government was unlikely to be straightforward. The party leaders in the Change bloc have to agree on a candidate for prime minister. They would also have to accept partnership with Arab parties, either in coalition or from outside. The rightwing opposition leader, Avigdor Lieberman, is said to be the most resistant. Joint List officials said it was unclear whether partnership with Palestinians really crossed Lieberman’s red lines, or whether he was just holding out for a top cabinet position.
Even before a new government could be formed, Jabareen argued, the 67 opponents of Netanyahu in the new Knesset could use their clear majority to wrest control of legislative power. “That would start by changing the speaker of the Knesset,” he said, adding that the opposition could also take control of the committee that oversees the legislative agenda.
“That could be very crucially important … even before we reach conclusions on the issue of a coalition and a new government,” he said, adding that one of the priorities of the new Knesset should be to repeal laws passed by the outgoing majority that infringed the independence of Israel’s judiciary.
To allow an opposition coalition to oust Netanyahu and function as a minority government, Jabareen made clear it would also have to address deep-seated inequality in Israeli society.
“We have suffered from systemic discrimination for years, so if Eisenkot speaks of change, I believe that the change should come also for our community. We need to be treated equally,” he said. “We also ask for a political horizon. We would like to see the war stopped and the resumption of negotiation with the Palestinian leadership. We would like to see a start of a change.”
The Joint List leader said he was concerned over what Netanyahu might do to keep his grip on power. The prime minister has already made allegations , without evidence, that the Arab parties had used Qatari funds illegally in the election campaign, which Jabareen dismissed as a bid to “delegitimise the political power of the Arab community” and “a dangerous incitement”.
One of Jabareen’s concerns was that the Israeli leader would join Donald Trump in the resumption of war on Iran as a pretext for putting off political transition.
“This is really a critical period,” he said. “There should be a clear voice from the opposition to go against any attempt by him to initiate war … or dictate a new military agenda in Israel.”

articles.title_orig: Deportees Turn to Social Media to Share Life in Countries They Barely Know
articles.title_zh: Deportees Turn to Social Media to Share Life in Countries They Barely Know
articles.content_orig:
“We are living through the greatest transformation that we have seen in our lifetimes, and likely for a significant time before that,” two-time Surgeon General Vivek Murthy told an audience at New York City’s flagship public library on Oct. 28, comparing the advent of artificial intelligence to the advent of nuclear weaponry in terms of the need for carefully thought out safety standards. “We're at a branch point,” he added. “What should the future really look like, what are we trying to protect and preserve?”
Murthy was not alone in sounding the alarm. Jim Steyer, founder and CEO of Common Sense Media , the organizer of the conference, told the mostly supportive crowd that recent history had proved that the industry leaders or, as he called them “tech broligarchs,” could not be relied upon to create digital information systems that were safe or healthy for children. “We did not get out in front of social media in time,” he told the gathering. “This is the moment. AI is a bigger deal. It's basically social media on steroids.”
New York’s governor Kathy Hochul seemed to underscore the point when she made an unscheduled stop at the daylong summit to announce new regulations around chatbots interactions with children. The bill was designed to ensure that AI agents do not impersonate humans or communicate in a way that suggests they have a relationship with a child. “It's happening so quickly,” said Hochul of the technological changes. “It's almost impossible for parents to know what's going on, for elected officials to stay ahead of it, and we certainly have learned the lesson that we can't count on the companies to put out products that are responsible and that put children first.”
Specifically, the new law, which goes into effect in January, will ban chatbots from encouraging suicide, self-harm, secrecy, or isolation and from discouraging children to seek help from other humans. They will also be banned from engaging in sexually explicit interactions and restricted from using a child’s past personal or health information in later conversations.
For the attendees and speakers at the summit, who ranged from Chelsea Clinton and Columbia law professor Tim Wu (onstage) to Uma Thurman (in the audience), the announcement was a good start, although many bemoaned the lack of federal regulation, around both AI and social media. “To this day, 2026, our federal government and Congress has still—nearly a quarter century after the advent of social media—failed to announce anything to protect our kids,” said Murthy, who is now chair of the advisory board of Common Sense Media’s Youth AI Safety Institute , which studies, tests, and rates AI platforms for children.
Panelists called for a range of protective and preventative remedies for what they described as the coming tsunami of AI, including requiring more data transparency from tech companies by enabling regulatory agencies and researchers to get more access to the information they’re holding, using consumer-protection laws to ensure that AI models have been rigorously tested for potential negative outcomes, adopting the European model of not allowing AI companies to deploy their platforms until they have proved they are safe, or even instituting criminal penalties for AI companies who unleash unsafe technologies. “As a former prosecutor, I can tell you one thing,” said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who earlier this month won a $25 billion judgment against Meta. “When you bring out handcuffs, suddenly everything changes.”
Not all the issues around AI can be solved by the law, however. One concern is the socialization of very young children by AI, including via voice-activated assistants like Alexa or very agreeable AI-enabled toys. “What do kids start to learn to expect from social practice? Do they expect someone to always agree with them? Is it always easy? Is it always like a transaction?” asked Dana Suskind , an early-childhood expert and professor at the University of Chicago. Human relationships are a lot messier, she noted. “They're chaotic, and that sort of mess is where a lot of learning happens.” Parents, who were caught off-guard by the influence of social media and digital devices, need to be educated about AI and encouraged that their imperfect parenting, as well as other human interaction, is vastly more beneficial to children than an AI companion, she said.
The summit also touched on the enormous implications AI is having on education and students’ ability to work and learn, when answers are in such ready supply. “MIT just did a report saying every assignment at MIT could be done by generative AI,” said John King, a former U.S. Secretary of Education and current chancellor of State University in New York. King is considering major changes to student assessment. “We have to make sure we are seeing the students do the work, and we have to make sure they're getting those foundational skills,” he said. “It literally means every faculty member reassessing what they assign and how they measure student learning.” And, as Clinton pointed out, this is an equity issue too. “We know that in families with less than $30,000 of household income, teenagers are three times more likely to either largely or entirely do their homework through artificial intelligence than those households with family incomes of $75,000 or more,” she said.
At the same time, students need to be prepared to enter a workforce in which AI skills are not optional. For those who have mastered them, the future is very bright. “The people coming in learn much more rapidly because AI gives them more capacity than they've had before,” said Gene Sykes, chairman of global mergers and acquisitions at Goldman Sachs of the banking giant’s new recruits. “So somebody, within a month, can be doing incredibly productive work.” If good education in AI is distributed unevenly, some graduates will be vastly better prepared for a career than others, further exacerbating wealth inequities.
While there was little consensus on the immediate steps to take as AI arrives, there was no argument that it will be consequential for children, families, and generations to come. “As we go into this age of transformation,” Murthy noted, “the question forced upon us is the following: What aspects of human existence do we want to protect and preserve at all costs?”
